title_r: Singing showed higher pitch, slower tempo and greater stability compared to conversation, and is associated with greater social bonding: A Registered Report replicating and extending Ozaki et al. (2024) with (NZ) English Speakers
abstract_r: Scientists have long debated the evolutionary functions of music and language. The Music and Social Bonding hypothesis proposes that music is particularly effective for strengthening cohesion in large groups because acoustic features that characterise song facilitate synchrony and promote social bonding. Ozaki and colleagues (2024) showed that singing exhibited a higher pitch, a slower temporal rate, and higher pitch stability, but their reliance on experienced musicians and a solo-singing format limited generalizability of their findings. This Registered Report compared singing with speaking within a single experimental paradigm, examining the relationship between group singing and conversation in Aotearoa New Zealand among 23 English-speaking participants. We analysed three acoustic features (pitch height, pitch stability, and temporal rate) and explored pre- and post-experiment changes in self-reported social bonding. Relative to conversation, singing showed higher pitch (d = 0.81, P = .0007, n=20), slower temporal rate (d = 1.14, P &lt; 1x10-9, n=20), and more stable pitch (d = 0.23, P = .006, n=20), replicating Ozaki et al.’s (2024) acoustic findings in a New Zealand English group context. Exploratory analyses suggested that social bonding increased more after singing (49% increase, n=8) than after conversation (26%, n=7) or lyric recitation (4%, n=8), though these results are tentative pending comparison with more global data. Our findings add support for acoustic and behavioral differences between song and speech, and highlight directions for future large-scale tests of the Music and Social Bonding hypothesis.

title_r: Materiality in the CSR-investor reaction relationship: A replication and extension of Flammer (2013)
abstract_r: We replicate and extend Flammer’s (2013) event study of investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility (CSR). Flammer found that investors reacted positively to eco-friendly events and negatively to eco-harmful events from 1980-2009 and that reaction to positive events decreased while reaction to negative events increased over time. We find similar results for Flamer’s original sample and an expanded sample including the same type of firms (U.S.-listed public firms) from 1980-2019. We then extend Flammer’s results by examining how materiality affects investor reaction over time. We find that investors only react to material events and that positive reaction to material eco-friendly events diminishes over time, while negative reaction to material eco-harmful events increases over time, suggesting that materiality is a key factor driving Flammer’s results.

title_r: Firm size and the use of export intermediaries. A replication study of Abel-Koch (The World Economy, 2013) (replication data)
abstract_r: This study replicates estimation results from Jennifer Abel-Koch, Who Uses Intermediaries in International trade? Evidence from Firm-level Survey Data, published in The World Economy (2013). In this paper she uses firm-level data from Turkey. The pure replication performed here that is based on a sample that differs only marginally from the sample used in the original study is successful. In addition to the pure replication I use firm-level data for Egypt from a highly similar survey. title_r: Inhibition-of-return-like effects in working memory? A preregistered replication study of Johnson et al. (2013)
abstract_r: The present study concerns a preregistered replication of the study conducted by Johnson et al. (2013), in which they showed an inhibition-of-return-like effect in working memory. Inhibition of return is a well-known phenomenon observed in the field of perception and refers to the observation that it takes longer to look back at a location that has recently been explored than to look at an unexplored location. Working memory is a central concept in the field of cognitive psychology and refers to the capacity to process and maintain information simultaneously over short periods of time. Johnson’s study applied the inhibition of return paradigm to the concept of working memory. Their results showed that it is harder to access a working memory representation that had just been thought of, i.e., refreshed, in comparison to an unrefreshed working memory representation. Contrary to this study of Johnson et al., who observed refreshing to result in inhibitory processes, most studies on refreshing have described its effect as increasing/prolonging the level of activation of the memory representations. In an attempt to integrate these opposite patterns produced by “refreshing”, we started by replicating one of the studies on inhibition of return in working memory reported by Johnson et al. (2013).

title_r: Precarity and conspiracy: a replication attempt of Adam-Troian et al. 2022
abstract_r: The study aims at replicating findings of the Adam-Troian et al. (2022) study on the mediating effect of institutional trust in the relationship between precarity and conspiracy beliefs (CBs). The study corroborated the view that the subjective experience of financial insecurity enhances the endorsement of CBs because precarity is associated with a decrease in institutional trust and institutional trust is among best-recognised antecedents of CBs. Before pre-registering the study, we obtained results from the first two datasets (two waves of a longitudinal study; the results will be reported as Studies 1a and 1b). The studies included two operationalisations of precarity: financial threat scale adapted to reflect Covid-related (wave 1 and 2) and war-related (wave 2) financial threats and subjective socio-economic status - a visual ladder task (Cantril, 1965). Institutional trust was measured as an average score of trust in eight institutions. Conspiracy beliefs were operationalised as general conspiracy mentality (Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire, Bruder et al., 2013) and specific conspiracy beliefs concerning COVID-19 (C19-UB, Teličák & Halama, n.d.). The results of Study 1a and Study 1b show congruence with the original Adam-Troian et al. (2022) findings. After consultations with the authors of the replicated study, we also checked the results robustness by adding sex, age and religiosity as covariates (see https://osf.io/kbr9s/ for details and preliminary results). Second, based on the data from two other representative Slovak samples (based on quota characteristics for gender, age, region, and education), we attempt to replicate the findings by Adam-Troian et al. (2021) at individual level in Study 2 and Study 3. Both datasets include subjective socio-economic status (a visual ladder task, Cantril, 1965) as a proxy of precarity. In Study 2, CBs were measured using the Conspiracy Thinking Scale (Uscinski et al., 2020) and trust was operationalised as confidence in the pandemic management and 3 items measuring trust in scientists, government and WHO. In Study 3, CBs were measured by 4 items (e.g., “Much of our lives are being controlled by plots hatched in secret places”) and trust was measured by 7 items. After obtaining results from all four Slovak datasets, we plan to perform a mini meta-analysis of the effects (Studies 1a/b–3). The data have been collected but not analysed prior to the registration. Finally, using the ESS10 (The European Social Survey Round 10) dataset, we attempt to replicate the original findings using high-quality international data on the subjective appraisal of economic situation (as an operationalisation of precarity), institutional trust measured as an average of trust in eight institutions and three questions capturing the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs (Study 4). The data have been collected but not analysed prior to the registration.

title_r: Precarity and conspiracy: a replication attempt of Adam-Troian et al. 2022
abstract_r: The study aims at replicating findings of the Adam-Troian et al. (2022) study on the mediating effect of institutional trust in the relationship between precarity and conspiracy beliefs (CBs). The study corroborated the view that the subjective experience of financial insecurity enhances the endorsement of CBs because precarity is associated with a decrease in institutional trust and institutional trust is among best-recognised antecedents of CBs. Before pre-registering the study, we obtained results from the first two datasets (two waves of a longitudinal study; the results will be reported as Studies 1a and 1b). The studies included two operationalisations of precarity: financial threat scale adapted to reflect Covid-related (wave 1 and 2) and war-related (wave 2) financial threats and subjective socio-economic status - a visual ladder task (Cantril, 1965). Institutional trust was measured as an average score of trust in eight institutions. Conspiracy beliefs were operationalised as general conspiracy mentality (Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire, Bruder et al., 2013) and specific conspiracy beliefs concerning COVID-19 (C19-UB, Teličák & Halama, n.d.). The results of Study 1a and Study 1b show congruence with the original Adam-Troian et al. (2022) findings. After consultations with the authors of the replicated study, we also checked the results robustness by adding sex, age and religiosity as covariates (see https://osf.io/kbr9s/ for details and preliminary results). Second, based on the data from two other representative Slovak samples (based on quota characteristics for gender, age, region, and education), we attempt to replicate the findings by Adam-Troian et al. (2021) at individual level in Study 2 and Study 3. Both datasets include subjective socio-economic status (a visual ladder task, Cantril, 1965) as a proxy of precarity. In Study 2, CBs were measured using the Conspiracy Thinking Scale (Uscinski et al., 2020) and trust was operationalised as confidence in the pandemic management and 3 items measuring trust in scientists, government and WHO. In Study 3, CBs were measured by 4 items (e.g., “Much of our lives are being controlled by plots hatched in secret places”) and trust was measured by 7 items. After obtaining results from all four Slovak datasets, we plan to perform a mini meta-analysis of the effects (Studies 1a/b–3). The data have been collected but not analysed prior to the registration. Finally, using the ESS10 (The European Social Survey Round 10) dataset, we attempt to replicate the original findings using high-quality international data on the subjective appraisal of economic situation (as an operationalisation of precarity), institutional trust measured as an average of trust in eight institutions and three questions capturing the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs (Study 4). The data have been collected but not analysed prior to the registration.

title_r: Klusowski et al (2021) replication and extension
abstract_r: Cognitive distortions in gambling scenarios may explain risks to disordered gambling – a recognised psychopathology in DSM-V with a similar harm profile to severe alcohol abuse disorder (Browne & Rockloff, 2017). Specifically, an illusion of control in which increased perceptions of control induce overestimations in winning prospects and overconfidence (Langer, 1975) has been implicated as a cognitive distortion common in disordered gamblers (Goodie & Fortune, 2013; Orgaz et al., 2013). However, recently this contribution has been challenged, for instance by failing to associate the illusion of control with disordered gambling behaviours such as increased wagering (Dannewitz & Weatherley, 2007; Moritz et al., 2021). These challenges have been further advanced by Klusowski et al. (2021). For example, in their final experiment (Experiment 17), a simple lottery task, these authors asked participants to give winning probability estimations for each of 3 equivalent boxes. They firstly found no illusion of control i.e., probability estimations were not higher in a condition where participants could choose their own box (post-choice condition), as opposed to having a box selected randomly for them (post-no-choice) or giving estimations prior to box selection (pre-selection). Therefore the manipulation of choice (active control) was not associated with increased irrational perceptions of winning. However, 26% of participants gave irrational probability estimates for any of the boxes exceeding ⅓ chance displayed as ‘non-uniform probabilistic beliefs’ in all 3 conditions. Consequently, this suggests the possibility of ‘passive’ cognitive distortions outside of the active distortions implicated by the illusion of control. Therefore, there is a need to replicate these findings, and extend them to attempt to find predictors of non-uniform probabilistic beliefs beyond the illusion of control. Gambling behaviour is one relevant potential predictor. In Western countries around half of the adult population gambles in any one year, and around 0.5-1% of the adult population may meet the diagnostic criteria for disordered gambling, a mental health condition in the DSM-5 (Potenza et al., 2019; Public Health England, 2021). Gamblers have many other cognitive distortions beyond the illusion of control, such as the gambler’s fallacy e.g., believing red is more likely to come up in roulette if multiple previous spins have come up black (Barron & Leider, 2010). Therefore, gambling participation and disordered gambling symptomology among gamblers may predict non-uniform probabilistic beliefs in this task. Additionally, research has found overlaps between characteristics associated with beliefs in superstition - irrational beliefs in the supernatural and its influence in affecting events; often manifesting as luck (Faiza, 2018) - and irrational gambling beliefs (Leonard & Williams, 2018; Williams et al., 2021). For example, beliefs in personal luck have been associated with increased perceptions in winning (Wohl & Enzle, 2002). This suggests that characteristics associated with superstition such as false attribution of cause and effect between unrelated events and unobjective assessments of probability may underlie cognitive distortions across both domains; gambling and superstition. Therefore, this may explain the correlations between superstition and problem gambling (Joukhador et al., 2004; Mowen et al., 2009; Pongsakornrungsilp et al., 2011) and identify superstition not only as a predictor of false probabilistic beliefs but problem gambling measures also. Nevertheless, superstition is a versatile set of beliefs wherein certain beliefs may not necessarily predict other superstitions. However, one factor of superstitious beliefs has been proposed is ‘passive superstition’ - beliefs that factors beyond one’s control affect outcomes (Hernandez et al., 2008). Indeed, this is associated with gambling e.g., lottery players often believe numbers based on lucky numbers or special dates are more likely to win (Hraba & Lee, 1995; Wang et al., 2016). It has also been associated with problem gambling behaviours such as risk-taking wherein the presence of magical objects increased the willingness for participants to enter more riskier gambling scenarios (Chinchanachokchai et al., 2016). Consequently, passive superstition may predict not only false probabilistic beliefs but problem gambling also. Additionally, passive superstition may be particularly relevant to alternatively explaining probability estimations in illusion of control paradigms as it encompasses beliefs that do not require senses that one’s own control will affect the likelihood of winning. Therefore, if passive superstition can predict false probability estimation it cannot necessarily be attributed to underlying beliefs that lead to illusions of control but a separate cognitive distortion beyond any choice component. This would strengthen conclusions that other cognitive distortions are relevant to illusion of control tasks. We will also attempt to address various limitations in Klusowski et al.’s Experiment 17. We plan to increase their sample size by approximately a factor of 5 to 3,000 participants. We will also use Bayesian over frequentist analysis given the hypothesised null effect of the experimental control manipulation. The original study was performed on MTurk, and some data suggests that Prolific is a rival crowdsourcing platform which provides more reliable data (Douglas et al., 2023). We will take further steps to ensure reliable data by excluding participants based on an attention check (which were collected but not used to exclude participants by Klusowski et al.), and by including a further seriousness check (Brühlmann et al., 2020).

title_r: What makes us lie: An online conceptual replication of Zhong, Bohns, and Gino (2010)
abstract_r: A previous study showed that darkness could increase fraud by creating a sense of “illusory anonymity” that lets individuals expect that they would be difficult to be perceived by others (Zhong et al., 2010). However, according to the conceptual metaphor theory (CMT), the alternative possibility that the results were caused by the White-Black metaphor could not be denied. In our earlier studies (Liu & Yamada, 2020a, 2020b), we did not find that the color metaphor factors (either the color of the screen background or the color of the team that participants belong to) could affect fraud. Additionally, we obtained a zero effect of colors by using two one-sided tests (TOST) in both the two studies. Before we conclude that the White-Black metaphor cannot influence fraud, we would like to confirm that fraud in the online task we used can be influenced by the room brightness employed by Zhong et al. In the present study, we try to let participants change the room brightness themselves (turning lights on/off in the night) by instructions and check fraud under different brightness conditions. It is foreseeable that some participants will not follow the instructions. However, if we can obtain an effect size to some degree (i.e. not a zero effect), we would conclude that the White-Black metaphor could not influence fraud, but the illusory anonymity account can be accepted.

title_r: Incidental Haptic Sensations May Not Influence Social Judgments: A Purely Confirmatory Replication Attempt of Study 1 by Ackerman, Nocera, & Bargh (2010)
abstract_r: This preregistered replication attempt focuses on the finding from Ackerman, Nocera, & Bargh (2010; ANB) that holding a heavy object triggers concepts related to importance. ANB reported that participants who were holding a heavy clipboard rated a job candidate as better overall and more seriously interested in the job than participants holding a light clipboard. We failed to replicate ANB’s results; instead, Bayes factor hypothesis tests indicated evidence for the absence of a difference between the heavy and the light condition in the overall evaluation andperceived seriousness of the candidate, and in participants’ perceived task importance. Our findings highlight the importance of conducting preregistered replication research and illustrate the theoretical and practical advantages of Bayesian inference in psychological research.

title_r: Effects of Labels on Face Recognition: Further Replication and Extension of Civile et al. (2019)
abstract_r: The face inversion effect refers to the impaired recognition of faces when they are presented upside down, as opposed to when they are presented right side up. A reduced face-inversion effect may suggest higher stigmatization or dehumanization of the faces being identified. This study seeks to extend prior work by Civile and colleagues (2019) and our initial replication of this work (pre-registered at https://osf.io/4ynp2). Together, these studies showed a decreased face inversion effect for faces labeled as "diagnosed with autism," as opposed to "regular people," suggesting that simply labeling individuals as diagnosed with autism has an effect on how those individuals are perceived. In the present study, we investigate whether different autism labels could differentially influence how the labeled individual is perceived.

title_r: Resource scarcity priming and face perception: A replication and extension of Study 1 of Rodeheffer et al. (2012) in Taiwan
abstract_r: Rodeheffer et al. (2012) showed that when people perceive resource scarcity, they are more likely to judge racially ambiguous people as out-group members. This research is important because it suggests that in-group narrowing due to resource scarcity can occur “unconsciously” in the “perception” stage, before attitudes and behaviors. However, there are two challenges regarding this finding: generalizability and replicability. To address these issues, we conduct replication research of Rodeheffer et al.'s (2012) Study 1 in Taiwan. Additionally, we aim to explore the mediators and moderators of the resource scarcity priming effect on face perception.

title_r: Direct replication of a research claim (Study 3) from Usta & Häubl (2011), in Journal of Marketing Research
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Usta & Häubl (2011) is that remembering a decision that a person delegated in the past depletes self-regulatory resources more than remembering an independently made decision (H3). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Moreover, when people remember a past decision that they delegated, their self-control is impaired more than when they remember a decision made independently (studies 3 and 4)." Participants were randomly assigned to one of two experimental conditions: They were asked to remember a past decision that they delegated or one that they made independently. In both conditions they were asked to briefly describe the decision and then describe the thoughts and feelings that experiencing the decision caused them to have. Participants were also shown pictures of two desserts (a chocolate cake and a fruit salad) and asked to indicate which one they would eat if they had the two desserts in front of them right then. All participants were administered a self-monitoring scale (Snyder, 1974) at the beginning of the study, and at the end, a past decision and consequences questionnaire and a PANAS scale (Watson, Clark and Tellegen, 1988). The measure of self-regulatory resource depletion in Study 3 was participants’ choice of dessert, which was analyzed with a logistic regression. A logistic regression analysis showed that the choice share of the chocolate cake among those who had been instructed to recall a delegated decision (70.6%) was significantly greater than among participants who had been asked to recall an independent decision (31.6%; χ2(1, 36) = 5.46, p < .03).

title_r: Independent Direct Replication #2 of Vess (2012, PS, Study 1)
abstract_r: The main goal of the current project is to execute an independent (direct) replication of Vess’ (2012, PS) main finding from his Study 1. Consistent with an embodiment account, he found that more anxiously attached individuals reported more desire for warm food and drinks, but only when such individuals had recalled a past romantic breakup (vs. recalling an ordinary event). We will execute a high-powered (estimated power of .95) independent replication using exactly the same measures, manipulations, instructions (exact instructions and manipulation acquired from Vess), and sampling approach (online sample using Amazon’s Mechanical Turk website). The primary goal is to determine whether Vess’ finding generalizes to a new sample of individuals, hence contributing to the question of whether Vess' original finding reflects reproducible knowledge.

(2005), who examined the association between the Behavioral Inhibition System (BIS), Behavioral Approach System (BAS) and trait anxiety on the neural processing of task irrelevant anger. title_r: Factors related to the questions parents ask during book reading: Replicating and extending Uscianowiski et al. (2020)
abstract_r: Parent-child book reading is an important context within children's early learning environment. Recent survey work has suggested that for preschool aged children, both parent (e.g., parent’s beliefs of their child’s understanding of mathematics) and child factors (e.g., child gender) are related to the types of questions parents ask during book number reading (Uscianowski et al., 2020). This work has suggested that parents ask more complex number-related questions on average of their sons than their daughters and that parents who rate their children as having more advanced number skills ask more complex number-related questions on average than parents who rate their children as less advanced. We will attempt to replicate these findings in a new sample, using the same materials. To directly extend this work we will not only consider the average-level of parent question complexity, but also consider the variation in the types of questions parents ask (i.e., the relation between these same factors and the variation in question complexity). We will also extend the broader work by investigating the types of questions parents ask during number books compared to non-number books and whether parent math anxiety or parent math enjoyment influence spontaneous number related focus during question asking. title_r: Fear generalization: a direct replication of Lissek et al. (2010)
abstract_r: Panic disorder is a prevalent and chronic anxiety disorder characterized by reoccurring panic attacks (Kessler et al., 2006). Panic attacks are sudden, often unexpected periods of intense fear, that can be accompanied by physical symptoms like sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, or others (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Fear is often caused by anxiety or the anticipation of danger. However, prior research has shown that such fear may not always be associated with only the stimuli that had been previously associated with a panic attack (e.g. getting a panic attack while being in the gym, so now the gym is predictive of a panic attack), but generalized to similar stimuli (e.g. all types of gyms). Lissek et al. (2010) have researched this fear generalisation and found that individuals diagnosed with panic disorder generalise fear more readily than healthy controls. Their findings led to numerous experimental and clinical studies, but no direct replication of this study has been done yet. However, replication of Lissek et al. (2010) is urgently needed for at least three reasons. First, an unpublished direct replication of the initial study design was unsuccessful. Second, Lissek et al.’s (2010) results are already being used in research that attempts to block or reduce fear generalization. Because of this, it is important to determine whether generalization has a role in panic disorder indeed and consequently whether relevant intervention studies may be useful for reducing panic symptomatology. Third, since a single lab replication is often not sufficient to assess the replicability of a study, the current research will replicate the study across multiple labs. In accordance with Lissek et al. (2010), we predict that participants with panic disorder will show more generalized avoidance compared to control subjects. Objective: The main goal of this research is to test whether individuals with a panic disorder diagnosis differ in the level of fear generalization compared to matched controls. This would be a direct replication of the seminal study by Lissek et al. (2010). Study design: This study will be a blinded between-subject study employing individuals with a panic diagnosis and healthy matched controls. Study population: Per clinic 25 individuals aged 18-65 with a prior diagnosis of a panic disorder and matched controls with no history of a mental disorder will be recruited, making a total of 50 individuals per clinic. Intervention: This study uses a fear generalization procedure consisting of three phases: pre-acquisition, fear acquisition, and a generalization test. In the pre-acquisition phase participants will see a small and a large circle, which will serve as the conditioned stimuli (CS). During the acquisition phase, the smallest and largest circles will serve as CS+ (the danger cue) and CS- (the safety cue), counterbalanced. One of these circles will be followed by shock administration (CS+), and the other circle is not followed by a shock (CS-). In the generalization test phase, participants see both CSs, as well as eight intermediate circles (generalization stimuli; GSs). Fear responses will be measured primarily by measuring startle responses, via electromyography (EMG), to a loud noise during the CS and GS presentations. Additionally, risk ratings as well as the accompanying reaction times (RT) will be collected by asking participants to estimate the level of risk during the experiment, with the available answers being 1 = no risk, 2 = moderate risk, and 3 = high risk. Main study parameters/endpoints: Electromyography (EMG) responses and reported risk ratings for each CS and GS. Online risk ratings and reaction time for the risk ratings. Both electromyograph responses and risk ratings will be used to test between-group differences in the course of learning. A self-report of anxiety levels after the main experiment will be used for testing between group differences. The Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Shear et al. 1997), State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (Spielberger et al. 1983) and Beck Depression Inventory (Beck et al. 1996) will be used to test for between group differences before the beginning of the study.

title_r: Does Scarcity Frame Value? Direct Replication of Shah et al. (2015)
abstract_r: In an influential article, Shah et al. (2015) hypothesized that resource scarcity weakens the effect of irrelevant contextual factors on economic valuations. In support, it was shown that the differences in the willingness to pay for a commodity depending on where it was purchased (a fancy hotel vs. a grocery store) and in the willingness to travel to receive a fixed discount depending on the size of the purchase (a cheap vs. an expensive computer) were smaller among the poor. The hypothesis that “scarcity frames value” is significant for the applicability of standard economic theories of rationality as well as the psychology of economic decisions. We will provide a large-scale direct replication of the key studies in the original article.

title_r: Selecting the special or choosing the common? A high-powered conceptual replication of Kim and Markus’ (1999) pen study
abstract_r: Kim and Markus (1999; Study 3) found that 74% of European Americans selected a pen with an uncommon (vs. common) color, whereas only 24% of East Asians made such a choice, highlighting a pronounced cross-cultural difference in the extent to which people opt for originality or make majority-based choices. The present high-powered study (N = 729) conceptually replicates the results from Kim and Markus (1999; Study 3), although our effect size (r = .12) is significantly weaker than that of the original study (r = .52). Interestingly, a larger proportion of Chinese, but not the US, participants selected a pen with an uncommon color now than during the original study. Thus, our findings indicate a potential transmission of certain western values to cultures traditionally characterized by collectivism and conformity, likely exacerbated by the globalization of mass media and the rapid economic growth in many East Asian countries.

title_r: Trends in U.S. Wage Inequality: Revising the Revisionists. A Replication Study of Autor, Katz, and Kearney (The Review of Economics and Statistics, 2008)
abstract_r: This paper successfully replicates Autor et al. (2008) and extends their analysis through 2022. The extension to an additional 17 years of analysis underscores the original finding that rising wage inequality was not an episodic event of the 1980s. That being said, overall 90/10 inequality and the college wage premium have plateaued since 2005. Despite overall inequality plateauing, uppertail 90/50 inequality has continued to increase since 1980 for both men and women. I also find that the composition-adjusted real wages of high school dropouts has caught up with high school graduates in the last decade. Between 2012 and 2022, high school dropouts saw larger real wage gains than any other education group. The combination of these findings is consistent with rising polarization in which employment and wages expand for high-wage and low-wage work.

title_r: Calibration information reduces bias during estimation of factorials: A (partial) replication and extension of Tversky and Kahneman (1973)
abstract_r: Tversky and Kahneman (1973) found that, under time pressure, people massively underestimated the expansion of 8! (correct value 40,320), and this bias was mitigated for participants presented the descending (8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1; Median=2,250) vs. ascending order (1x2x3x4x5x6x7x8; Median=512). In a first-ever replication (N=140), we also found predominant underestimation, but no significant between-subjects descending vs. ascending order effect. However, when participants then estimated the opposite order, we reproduced this order effect within-subjects. Finally, participants received calibration information (the correct value of 6! or 10!) and again estimated both orders of 8!. Participants who received 10! made more accurate estimates for 8! (Median=38,000), which did not differ statistically from the correct value. Participants who received 6! still grossly underestimated (Median=2,678.5), despite 8! being closer to 6! than 10! in linear and log units. Thus, we surprisingly found the classic factorial estimation bias only within-subjects, and provide evidence for how calibration can reduce it.

title_r: Modeling Help Seeking Intentions In Victims Of Intimate Partner Violence: A Conceptual Replication Of Fleming And Resick (2017)
abstract_r: Victims of intimate partner violence come forward and seek services and help for the crimes committed upon them at much lower rates than victims of other interpersonal crimes. In this study, the Theory of Planned Behavior was used to assess individual behavioral predictors of formal help-seeking in victims of intimate partner violence in order to better understand factors that promote or inhibit help-seeking in this vulnerable population, including victims’ attitudes about help seeking, the subjective norms they feel about help seeking, their perceived ability to get help, and the relationship these factors have with prior experiences. Partial support was found for the full Theory of Planned Behavior model predicting intentions for all resource types, with attitudes and perceived behavioral control predicting intentions for most resources, while norms rarely contributed to the variance. Prior experience was related to attitudes about several of the resources.

title_r: Multiple Aspects and Correlates of Body Figure Ratings: A Replication and Extension of Fallon and Rozin (1985)
abstract_r: College females, using a set of nine figure drawings reflecting very thin to very heavy figures, rated their current figure (based on how they thought they looked versus how they felt), ideal figure, how they appeared to others, and the figure they deemed most attractive to men. A subsample of the 123 subjects also completed measures of body satisfaction, depression, eating disturbance, teasing, and noted the age of menarche. The results replicated and extended the findings of Fallon and Rozin (1985), who found that ideal figures were smaller than ratings of current size. Additionally, there was a significant difference between the two protocols for current size, indicating that subjects rated their size as larger when asked to rate based on affective instructions. Figure ratings based on cognitive/rational instructions did not differ from those based on how they conceptualized others' views of their bodies. Significant correlations were observed among figure ratings, body satisfaction, eating disturbance, depression, and teasing. The need to focus on etiological mechanisms of disturbed body image and eating behavior is addressed, and the role of teasing as a possible precipitant is examined.

title_r: The Possible Unemployment Cost of Average Inflation Below a Credible Target. A Replication Study of Svensson (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2015). Data.
abstract_r: These are the replication files for Oraby (JCRE, 2022). The paper aims to replicate Svensson (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2015). Abstract: This paper replicates the main analysis of Svensson (2015) with some expansion to the original analysis, mainly for the United States. Overall, the replication exercise successfully confirms the conclusions of Svensson (2015). In both Sweden and the United States, empirical evidence supports the existence of a non-vertical long run Phillips curve. The slope of the long run Phillips curve recorded -0.75 in Sweden and -0.23 in the United States. While the average inflation rate in the United States was very close to its targeted level, the average inflation rate in Sweden was 0.6 percentage points below its targeted level over the sample period. The deviation of inflation rate from its targeted level in Sweden resulted in an unemployment cost equivalent to 0.8 percentage points over the sample period where the average unemployment rate recorded 7.4 percent compared with an estimated 6.6 percent had the average inflation rate been at its targeted level.

title_r: Productivity premia for many modes of internationalization. A replication study of Békés and Muraközy (Economics Letters, 2016) (replication study)
abstract_r: This study attempts to replicate estimation results from Gábor Békés and Balázs Muraközy, Measuring productivity premia with many modes of internationalization, published in Economics Letters (2016). In this paper the authors use comparable firm-level data for seven European countries based on the EFIGE dataset to estimate the productivity premia of firms with various modes of internationalization by several empirical methods to demonstrate how results differ due to the method applied. While the EFIGE data are available free of charge from the web one core variable used by Békés and Muraközy is not, because total factor productivity (tfp) as computed by the authors is based on data from a commercial data base and, therefore, is available for users with a license to this database only. The freely available EFIGE data, however, come with another tfp-variable that can be used instead. In this replication study I use the EFIGE data with this publicly available tfp-variable to replicate (parts of) the estimations of Békés and Muraközy (2016) to see whether their results hold with the widely used public use version of the EFIGE data, too. It turns out that the big picture that emerges from using both productivity measures tends to be very similar. The use of the public use version of the EFIGE data for empirical investigations that deal with productivity, therefore, seems to be feasible.

title_r: Trends in U.S.Wage Inequality: Revising the Revisionists. A Replication Study of Autor, Katz, and Kearney (The Review of Economics and Statistics, 2008)
abstract_r: Summary: These codes replicate Autor et al. (2008) and extend their analysis through 2022. Findings: The extension to an additional 17 years of analysis underscores the original finding that rising wage inequality was not an episodic event of the 1980s. That being said, overall 90/10 inequality and the college wage premium have plateaued since 2005. Despite overall inequality plateauing, upper-tail 90/50 inequality has continued to increase since 1980 for both men and women. I also find that the composition-adjusted real wages of high school dropouts has caught up with high school graduates in the last decade. Between 2012 and 2022, high school dropouts saw larger real wage gains than any other education group. The combination of these findings is consistent with rising polarization in which employment and wages expand for high-wage and low-wage work.

title_r: The Long-Term Effects of Measles Vaccination on Earnings and Employment. A Replication Study of Atwood (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2022)
abstract_r: The replication package reproduces the results presented in the paper "The Long-Term Effects of Measles Vaccination on Earnings and Employment. A Replication Study of Atwood (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2022)" by Mara Barschkett, Mathias Huebener, Andreas Leibing, Jan Marcus and Shushanik Margaryan, published in: Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, Volume 2, 2023-4. Data are available at http://doi.org/10.3886/E138401V1. Abstract: Atwood analyzes the effects of the 1963 U.S. measles vaccination on long-run labor market outcomes, using a generalized difference-in-differences approach. We reproduce the results of this paper and perform a battery of robustness checks. Overall, we confirm that the measles vaccination had positive labor market effects. While the negative effect on the likelihood of living in poverty and the positive effect on the probability of being employed are very robust across the different specifications, the headline estimate—the effect on earnings—is more sensitive to the exclusion of certain regions and survey years.

title_r: Replicating and extending Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011, Exp. 2)
abstract_r: Introduction: Framing refers to how information is presented and structured in communication (Goffman, 1974)—what aspects are emphasized, how issues are categorized, and what language choices are made. Linguistic framing can significantly shape perception, emotion, and behavior, particularly in public discourse. Even minor changes in wording can influence people's interpretations and decisions, especially when those changes involve metaphorical language (Brugman et al., 2019; Flusberg et al., 2024). A seminal study by Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011) demonstrated that metaphorical frames can guide reasoning about social issues. In their experiments, participants were presented with a description of a crime problem framed either as a "beast preying on the city" or a "virus infecting the city." The type of metaphor affected participants' policy preferences: the "beast" metaphor led to more punitive, enforcement-focused solutions, while the "virus" metaphor elicited support for reform-oriented interventions. Notably, participants were often unaware of the metaphor’s influence on their thinking. However, as Flusberg et al. (2024) point out, the effects of metaphorical framing should not be assumed to generalize across cultures, historical periods, or languages. Moreover, in light of the ongoing replication crisis in psychology, it is essential to test the robustness of such findings (Camerer et al., 2018). Several replication attempts have yielded mixed results. For instance, Christmann and Göhring (2016) observed similar effects in a German-speaking sample, although some methodological differences were present. In contrast, Steen et al. (2013), who included additional controls, found no significant metaphor effects—raising questions about the specific conditions under which metaphorical framing is effective. Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2015) later responded with further analyses, clarifying aspects of the original findings and addressing key criticisms. The present study aims to contribute to this body of research by replicating and extending the original Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011, Exp. 2) work. It investigates not only whether metaphorical framing reliably influences reasoning about crime, but also whether this effect generalizes across different populations or is moderated by some individual or contextual variables. By addressing inconsistencies in prior replication efforts, this study seeks to offer a more comprehensive understanding of how metaphor shapes human reasoning about complex societal issues. Methods Ethics statement The study will adhere to the ethical standards for research with human participants and has received approval from the Ethics Committee at the University of Granada with the approval number: 3788/CEIH/2023. Informed consent will be obtained from all participants before they take part in the study, and all participant data will be anonymous. Participants For this experiment, we used G*Power version 3.1.9.7 to estimate the sample size required for a 2 X 2 chi-squared test with 1 degree of freedom, alpha of .05, and power of 90%. We selected a power of 90% rather than 80%, as recommended by Lakens (2022), to reduce the risk of Type II errors in replication studies. The first two free-response format questions in this study were designed to closely follow Experiment 2 of Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011), who reported an effect size of .209 (Cohen’s w). However, since we also included a binary forced-choice question (see “Materials and procedure” section), we preferred to use the more conservative effect size (Cohen’s w = .14) reported by Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2015). This effect size corresponds to the pooled data from their first experiment and Experiment 4 of Steen et al.’s (2014), in which participants (N = 876) were presented with a five options forced-choice question. We chose not to use the effect size from the binary forced-choice question in Thibodeau and Boroditsky’s (2015) second experiment, as it included the term “patrols” as a response option and it has already been demonstrated that the role of a police officer is ambiguous (Thibodeau & Boroditsky, 2011). As a result, we established the minimum usable sample size in 537 participants. As our experiment is online and we expect to have 25% attrition rate after applying exclusion criteria (see below), we will recruit 672 participants. Additional participants may be recruited until reaching the minimum sample size of N = 672. Participants will be recruited through two platforms: Prolific (https://www.prolific.com) and the SONA platform of the Mind, Brain and Behavior Research Center of the University of Granada (https://ugr-cimcyc.sona-systems.com). Both platforms ensure the anonymity of the participants. Inclusion criteria for participation are as follows: • Participants must be 18 years old or older. • Participants must be native Spanish speakers and living in Spain, to reduce the risk of language proficiency and culture becoming a confounding factor (for a review, see Flusberg et al., 2024). Exclusion Criteria Additionally, we will exclude: • Participants who participate in the study more than once. • Participants who complete the survey in an amount of time deemed too long (more than 10 minutes) or short (less than 1 minute), as this may indicate a lack of engagement with the task. • Participants who do not respond correctly to a verification question included at the end of the survey. • Participants who do not complete all required questions, provide responses that are unintelligible, impossible to code in one of the two categories (“enforce” or “reform”, see below) or irrelevant. Materials and procedure The questionnaire will be programmed and run on the LimeSurvey platform of the University of Granada. The procedure will closely replicate that of Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011, Experiment 2). Participants will be redirected from Prolific or SONA to the LimeSurvey questionnaire. After providing informed consent, participants will be randomly assigned to either the "crime-as-beast" or "crime-as-virus" condition (see below). They will then be instructed to read a short news report followed by short questions on its content. The short news report will be preceded by the following warning: “Lee el texto con atención porque cuando pases a la siguiente pantalla, ya no podrás volver a él.” [Read the text carefully because once you move to the next screen, you will not be able to go back to it.]. The short news report will be a text describing the crime problem in the fictional city of Carballa. This text and the three questions presented afterwards have been directly translated into Spanish from the materials used in the original study by Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011). The original English text was translated into Spanish using a multi-step process to ensure accuracy and cultural appropriateness. Firstly, two bilingual speakers (MO and JPGS) of English and Spanish independently translated the text into Spanish. A third bilingual speaker of English and native Spanish speaker (JS) reviewed both translations and created a single revised version. The final Spanish translation was then reviewed and approved by an expert in English philology (JVM). Finally, an English native speaker who is also a Spanish-English bilingual and was unaware of the topic of this study when translating the texts (AA), carried out a backward translation. All the authors of this study agreed that the original and the backward translated text were conceptually similar. This rigorous translation process aims at minimizing any potential confounding effects due to translation. All materials produced during this translation process can be found in the data repository. The finalized text describing the crime problem in the fictional city of Carballa that participants will read is: “El crimen es un/a {bestia/virus} que asola la ciudad de Carballa. Hasta hace cinco años, Carballa estaba en buen estado, sin vulnerabilidades evidentes. Desafortunadamente, en los últimos cinco años, las defensas de la ciudad se han debilitado y la ciudad ha sucumbido al crimen. Actualmente hay más de 55.000 incidentes delictivos al año – con un aumento de más de 10.000 por año. Hay una preocupación de que, si la ciudad no recupera su fortaleza pronto, puedan comenzar a desarrollarse problemas aún más graves.” [Crime is a {beast/virus} ravaging the city of Carballa. Five years ago Carballa was in good shape, with no obvious vulnerabilities. Unfortunately, in the past five years the city’s defense systems have weakened, and the city has succumbed to crime. Today, there are more than 55,000 criminal incidents a year – up more than 10,000 per year. There is a worry that if the city does not regain its strength soon, even more serious problems may start to develop.] After reading the text, participants will press a button to continue, and they will be unable to go back to the previous screen. title_r: Close and Conceptual Replications of Waytz, Dungan, & Young (2013) Studies 2b and 4
abstract_r: Waytz, Dungan, and Young (2013) conducted four studies to test the hypothesis that valuing fairness over loyalty is more strongly associated with willingness to blow the whistle on transgressors than valuing loyalty over fairness. title_r: Replication and extension of Blini et al. (2013): Different effects of numerical magnitude on visual and proprioceptive reference frames
abstract_r: The main aim of this project is to replicate the study of Blini et al. (2013) in order to evaluate the effect of listening numbers of different magnitude on the signed errors of the visual rod bisection (RB) task and proprioceptive straight-ahead (SA) task. Blini et al. title_r: The effect of order-label training on generalization, a replication study of Ramscar et al., (2010)
abstract_r: In this preregistration we describe a detailed plan to replicate Ramscar et al. (2010) paper about the effect of the order of presentation of feature-label pair association on symbolic learning. We attempt an exact replication of the original study except (1) that the participants are recruited and tested online and (2) a further task is added at the end of the experiment. We will also looking at the data from the original two test tasks separately, as well as combined, in order to further elucidate the nature of these tasks. The experiment is a word learning experiment in which participants learn associations between pictures of novel objects and written labels (e.g. wug). Critically, there are two learning-conditions – in the feature-label condition pictures are presented before labels, in the feature-label condition labels are presented before pictures. In both conditions there are three labels which are associated with six classes of fribbles, with each subcategory of fribbles having a set of discriminating features (Figure 1, circled features). However, critically, 1.1. 2.1 and 3.1 (high-frequency items) are encountered three times as often as subcategories 1.2 2.2 and 3.2 (low frequency items) (there is also a fourth “easy” control category of blue fribbles). Due to the way that body shape is shared across subcategories, it can be seen that for low frequency items, body shape is a high salience feature which has been strong associated with an alternative label to the correct label. According to discriminative learning theory, participants in the feature-label condition should be better able to ignore shape and learn the discriminating features which determine which labels should be used. Following Ramscar et al., (2010) after exposure to the language, we include 2AFC tests testing generalization where participants had to choose which of four novel fribbles went with a label/ which of four labels went with a novel fribble. We also follow this with a new contingency judgment task that links the theoretical predictions about the resulting learning weights from error-driven learning, to the participants’ ratings behaviour of the feature-label association plausibility. The participants’ judgment is predicted to roughly reflect the learning weights of the model when learning is completed. We expect that this pre-registration will establish (1) a robust paradigm that can be used as starting point for future studies online, (2) a sensitive task capturing estimates of learning weights across participants, providing a direct comparison to the predictions based on the RW model (Rescorla, Wagner, and others (1972)). We base our predictions on Ramscar et al., (2010), although our predicted effect sizes are based on data from an unpublished study that replicates Ramscar et al., (2010) effects* , and – for the additional contingency task – from our own pilot data. Our primary research question is as follows: Does Feature-Label-Ordering affect discrimination learning? In particular, when participants are confronted with novel exemplars, is there an advantage in terms of generalization of predictive cues for feature-label over label-feature in the low frequency condition? ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ * The reason we use this data rather than from the published study is that we have it available in a format where it is possible to run the necessary logistic mixed effect models to obtain our predicted effects

title_r: Replication Study: Google Effects on Memory, Exp. 2 (Sparrow et al., 2011)
abstract_r: The aim of this study is to replicate the findings of experiment 2 conducted by Sparrow et al. (2011) regarding the transactive memory theory and, specifically, the Google effect on memory. The experiment was designed to be an exact replication of the original study with minor changes to setting and materials. In the original experiment, participants first had to type a number of trivia statements and later completed a free recall memory task as well as a recognition task. The study followed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design. Half of the participants were instructed to try to remember the statements, whilst the other half did not receive explicit memory instructions. In addition, in each memory condition, half of the participants believed the computer would save the typed statements for later access and the other half were told the statements were deleted after typing. Those participants who thought the typed statements would be erased remembered more statements in the free recall condition than participants thinking the statements were saved for later access. In addition, an interaction effect was found in the recognition task. Participants who were instructed to remember the statements in the erased-condition had the best recognition, whereas those who were told to remember the statements in the saved-condition had the worst recognition performance. The memory for those who were not explicitly told to remember the statements fell in between those other two conditions.

title_r: Direct replication of Staw (1976)
abstract_r: Escalation of commitment refers to the decision error in which people stick to their original decision despite negative feedback (Sleesman, Conlon, McNamara & Miles, 2012; Staw, 1976; Staw & Fox, 1977). In 1976, Staw initiated experimental research on escalating commitment. In his study Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy: A Study of Escalating Commitment to a Chosen Course of Action, he showed that escalation was particularly pronounced when people were personally responsible for negative decision consequences. The interaction between responsibility and consequence was significant (p = <.019). Since then, there have been numerous studies investigating the escalation of commitment and the underlying effects. The findings are ambivalent, as the results often do not match or even contradict those of Staw (1976). There are many studies that used Staw's (1976) stimulus material, the A&S Financial Decision Case, or were based on his approach (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Armstrong, Coviello & Safranek, 1993; Bialek, Węgrzyn, & Meyers, 2021; Conlon & Parks, 1987; McCain, 1986; Morgan & Hansen, 2006; Pfeiffer, Schönborn, Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt, 2007; Schoorman & Holahan, 1996; Schoorman, Mayer, Douglas & Hetrick, 1994; Singer, 1990; Singer & Singer, 1986). However, these studies did not test the interaction effect responsibility x consequence (Armstrong et al., 1993) and altered or excluded relevant aspects of the paradigm. For example, a different scenario and other variables were examined (Negrini, Riedl & Wibral, 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007) or the methodological approach was changed (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Bialek et al., 2021; Singer & Singer, 1986). For this reason, the planned study in the form of a direct replication should provide information on how robust and reliable Staw's (1976) results are if there are as few deviations as possible from the original study. Of particular interest is the replicability of the interaction effect personal responsibility x decision consequences. In addition, the reasons for the investment decisions are evaluated using content analysis. Armstrong et al. (1993) asked the participants to justify their decision, but did not analyze this. Other studies did not even include the justification in their design (Bialek et al., 2021; Negrini et al., 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007; Singer & Singer, 1986). The planned study therefore extends the existing literature with a replication of the study by Staw (1976), which not only records the participants' reasons for their decisions, but also evaluates them using content analysis.

title_r: Testing the interleaving effect without response bias: A preregistered replication of Kornell & Bjork (2008)
abstract_r: Our proposed high-powered, preregistered study aims to rigorously replicate and extend Kornell & Bjork (2008) by conducting a (1) direct replication and (2) a version of the task implementing a forced-choice (2AFC) procedure – the gold standard in memory testing. We argue that Kornell and Bjork (2008) and previous replications have used a testing procedure that allows for the influence of response bias, which may confound estimates of memory strength. Our proposed study aims to replicate Kornell & Bjork’s original study and extend it by implementing a forced-choice procedure – which sidesteps response bias – and comparing the results using these two different measurement techniques.

title_r: The opportunity cost of time modulates cognitive effort – a replication study of Otto & Daw (2019) Neuropsychologia
abstract_r: It has been shown that there are different decision-making strategies: fast but error-prone heuristic decision-making, and slower but more accurate deliberative decision-making (Balleine & Dickinson, 1998; Daw, Gershman, Deymour, Dayan, & Dolan, 2011; Dolan & Dayan, 2013). While deliberative responding leads to more appropriate responses, it also requires more computational time, during which cognitive resources cannot be used for other computations that could lead to reward. It has been proposed that the brain approximates such opportunity costs of time by calculating the average reward rate of the environment (Niv, Daw, Joel, & Dayan, 2007). Using three experiments, Otto & Daw (2019) provide evidence that when the opportunity cost of time is higher, subjects make more mistakes and respond faster. These results therefore suggest that a higher average reward rate in the environment causes a shift towards more heuristic responding (Otto & Daw, 2019). I aim to reproduce these results using one of the experiments used by Otto and Daw (2019), namely a Simon task.

title_r: Does Telling a Story in Reverse Elicit Cues to Deceit? A Replication and Extension of Vrij, Leal, Mann, and Fisher (2012)
abstract_r: Purpose The reverse order recall technique has been suggested as tool to improve deception detection accuracy (Vrij et al., 2008). Systematic reviews of cognitive approaches to deception have focused on detection judgements (Mac Giolla & Luke, 2020; Vrij et al., 2017) and not the cues judges are theoretically relying on to make such decisions. Yet, findings regarding the cues these techniques provoke are inconsistent. Thus, we will conduct a registered replication of Vrij et al., 2012, focusing on the cues the reverse order produces in senders. We will also investigate the link between cues and judgments, to provide a stronger theoretical basis for the technique. Methods Following Vrij et al., 2012, in Experiment 1, participants will complete one of two missions that they will be interviewed about twice, once lying and once telling the truth. Interviewers will ask participants to recount their experience in chronological and reverse order. We will then code these interviews for cues associated with deception according to a cognitive approach. In Experiment 2, participants will either view two videos of the senders or read two transcripts from Experiment 1 and will decide whether they are lying or telling the truth. Responses will submitted to a lens model mediation analysis to assess the link between production and utilization of cues.

title_r: Effect of Losses and Gains on Working Memory Performance: A replication and extension of Massar et al 2020 Front Hum Neurosci (effort-based decision making and performance)
abstract_r: Human decision-making is often driven by a motivation to avoid losses than to pursue gains, a phenomenon called loss aversion. Based on our previously published study (Massar et al., 2020, Exp3), loss incentives motivated participants more than gains in working memory performance at the highest level of N-back we tested, the 4-Back. We aim to replicate and extend the study with a larger sample size to verify whether results still hold. Specifically, we discovered that loss incentives motivated performance more than the gains incentive on the 4-back task, and we wish to verify this finding with a larger sample size. This finding had surprised us, considering that there have been no consistent results on this matter in the literature (e.g. Carsten et al 2019; Belayachi et a. 2015). Even in our previously published study, there was no consistent finding because losses did not motivate performance in the motivated vigilance task (Massar et al 2020, Exp1&2), as losses did in the N-back task, so we aim to test whether our previous findings on the working memory task are valid. Furthermore, as an innovative addition, we intend on incorporating pupillometry as a measure of physiological effort into our N-back study design so that we can test whether pupil diameter changes during loss versus gain conditions.

title_r: Ku_JournEnvPsych_2014_YpZZ - RRTeam_Caldwell & Vaughn - Direct Replication
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Study 1 of Ku and Zaroff (2014) is that higher I/E participants [intrinsic relative to extrinsic values scores] would show higher willingness to pay to protect the environment. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "In both 169 university students (M = 21.11, SD = 1.10) and 347 adults (M = 31.65, SD = 14.48) of Chinese ethnicity, the higher endorsement of intrinsic relative to extrinsic values was indeed related to a higher willingness to pay to protect the environment (Studies 1 and 2)...". The claim is tested by comparing the mean WTP (willingness to pay) score in the relative intrinsic group and the relative extrinsic group. As a whole, the hypothesis was supported as the relative intrinsic group obtained a mean score of 4.01 (SD = .71) on the WTP (willingness to pay), which was significantly higher than the relative extrinsic group's mean score of 3.30 (SD = .59), t(79) = 4.87, p < .001, r = .48. Note: When we replicated the original authors’ analyses using their dataset, we discovered an error in the published results: the above standard deviations had been switched. None of the other results of this analysis changed. These are the correct results: As a whole, the hypothesis was supported as the relative intrinsic group obtained a mean score of 4.01 (SD = .59) on the WTP (willingness to pay), which was significantly higher than the relative extrinsic group's mean score of 3.30 (SD = .71), t(79) = 4.87, p < .001, r = .48.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Mussweiler and Strack (2000, Study 2) Using Temperature Anchoring and a Season-Related LDT
abstract_r: This study conceptually replicates Study 2 by Mussweiler and Strack (2000), which tested the Selective Accessibility Model (SAM) of the anchoring effect. According to SAM, anchoring occurs through the selective activation of anchor-consistent knowledge, driven by hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. In the original study, participants first completed a standard comparative anchoring task (judging whether the average price of a new car was higher or lower than U.S. $11,000 or $22,000), followed by a Lexical Decision Task (LDT). After the LDT, they estimated the average price of a new car in an absolute judgment task. The results supported SAM, demonstrating a significant interaction between anchor condition and word type in the LDT. In the present study, we conducted a conceptual replication of this design, using an anchoring task involving temperature estimates and an LDT employing season-related words (summer- and winter-related words).

title_r: Winning Hearts and Minds in Online Surveys: Replication and Extension of Searles and Mattes (2015)
abstract_r: How can we best induce emotions in online survey experiments? This project measures the effectiveness of eight anger inductions (three of which replicate treatments from Searles and Mattes 2015) and six gratitude inductions in the context of an online survey. Many emotion induction treatments have been used and/or validated in offline settings (see Searles and Mattes 2015 for validation of scenario vignettes, self-statements, and images; see also Young 2019 for examples of autobiographical emotional memory tasks). However, political scientists regularly study the effect of emotions using online survey experiments (e.g., Webster, Connors and Sinclair 2022), where participants are frequently inattentive and distracted (Ternovski and Orr 2022), potentially weakening treatment effects (Clifford and Jerit 2014). This project builds on the methodological literature on emotion induction by validating emotion induction techniques—including scenario vignettes, self-statements, images, and autobiographical emotional memory tasks (AEMTs)—for online contexts. We also introduce a deliberately bundled “two-step” AEMT treatment that asks people to recast the valence that they attach to emotional memories. This novel treatment is designed to reproduce the experience of specifically political emotions. In developing this treatment, we seek to test the microfoundations of emotional experiences prompted by propaganda and political persuasion. We will also, in the project, test reactions to research participation among participants, building on Weiss (2024). This analysis takes advantage of the set-up of the experiment, where we are priming both negative and positive emotions and doing so—in one treatment group—by using negative images. In this case, we are interested in confirming the expectations of a largely non-experimental literature on reactions to research participation, which would suggest that participants do not become significantly more distressed or resentful when participating in research that involves negative content versus neutral or positive content.

title_r: Cutright_JournConsRes_2011_eg3p - Baskin - Direct Replication - yyy1
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Cutright et al (2011) is the Experiment 5 claim that individuals measured to be low (vs. high) in system confidence respond differently to the opportunity to directly vs. indirectly support the system through a choice of national vs. international T-shirt: when provided with a chance for indirect support, low- (but not high) confidence individuals will respond to a threat by selecting national brands; when provided with a chance to directly support the system, the pattern will reverse such that high-confidence individuals only will respond to a threat by choosing the national brand T-shirt. This claim is based on the following sentence from the paper’s abstract: ““[W]hen an important system is (verbally) attacked, individuals who are the least confident in the legitimacy of the system seek and appreciate consumption choices that allow them to indirectly and subtly defend the system, [while] individuals who are highly confident in the system … seek consumption choices that allow them to defend the system in direct and explicit ways.”” The claim is tested with a repeated-measures logistic regression (three choices per participant) on T-shirt choice (national vs. international) with threat condition (high/none), the system confidence measure, and type of national brand (direct/indirect support) as predictors. This analysis found a three-way interaction of threat condition (high threat vs. no threat), system confidence, and type of brand (direct vs. indirect support), B = -1.29, Z = -3.15, p < 0.01.

title_r: Direct replication of a research claim from Ku and Zaroff (2014), from the Journal of Environmental Psychology
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Study 1 of Ku and Zaroff (2014) is that higher I/E participants [intrinsic relative to extrinsic values scores] would show higher willingness to pay to protect the environment. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "In both 169 university students (M = 21.11, SD = 1.10) and 347 adults (M = 31.65, SD = 14.48) of Chinese ethnicity, the higher endorsement of intrinsic relative to extrinsic values was indeed related to a higher willingness to pay to protect the environment (Studies 1 and 2)...". The claim is tested by comparing the mean WTP (willingness to pay) score in the relative intrinsic group and the relative extrinsic group. As a whole, the hypothesis was supported as the relative intrinsic group obtained a mean score of 4.01 (SD = .71) on the WTP (willingness to pay), which was significantly higher than the relative extrinsic group's mean score of 3.30 (SD = .59), t(79) = 4.87, p < .001, r = .48. Note: When we replicated the original authors’ analyses using their dataset, we discovered an error in the published results: the above standard deviations had been switched. None of the other results of this analysis changed. These are the correct results: As a whole, the hypothesis was supported as the relative intrinsic group obtained a mean score of 4.01 (SD = .59) on the WTP (willingness to pay), which was significantly higher than the relative extrinsic group's mean score of 3.30 (SD = .71), t(79) = 4.87, p < .001, r = .48.

title_r: Is There a Positive Association between Working Memory Capacity and Mind Wandering in a Low-Demand Breathing Task? A Preregistered Replication of Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012)
abstract_r: Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012, Experiment 2) found that working memory capacity (WMC) correlated positively with mind-wandering propensity measured by thought probes in a breath-monitoring task, but was unassociated with the tendency to self-catch mind-wandering. Here, I sought to replicate the associations between mind-wandering and WMC in the Levinson et al. breath task. With data from a large sample of subjects and two measures of WMC, the data from the current study suggests that, if WMC correlates with probe-caught mind wandering, it is most likely negative. In addition, the evidence regarding self-caught mind wandering is consistent with Levinson et al. for the sum of self-caught responses, but when self-caught responses are considered in proportion to probe-caught mind wandering, modest evidence was found for a positive association with WMC.

title_r: Does priming analytic thinking reduce conspiracy beliefs? High-powered preregistered replications of Study 2 and Study 4 from Swami et al. (2014)
abstract_r: Analytic thinking is reliably associated with lower belief in conspiracy theories. However, evidence for whether increasing analytic thinking can reduce belief in conspiracies is sparse. As an exception to this, Swami et al. (2014) showed that priming analytical thinking through a verbal fluency task (i.e., scrambled sentence task) or a processing fluency manipulation (i.e., difficult-to-read fonts) reduces belief in conspiracy theories. While these studies are the most cited experimental research on reducing belief in conspiracy theories, they are yet to be replicated. To probe the robustness of these effects, we propose two preregistered, highly powered (i.e., 95%) direct replications of two of the original studies (i.e., Studies 2 and 4). As such, the proposed studies have the potential to contribute to the robustness of experimental research on belief in conspiracies, as well as to inform urgently needed insights on ways to reduce it.

title_r: Direct Replication of a Research Claim from Yang et al. (2013), from the Journal of Marketing Research
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the main claim reported in Yang et al.’s (2013) experiment 1. The authors reported that the more a prospect’s frame was associated with risk, the less buyers were willing to pay for that prospect: Framing a risky prospect as a “lottery ticket” compared with a “gift card” reduced participants’ willingness to pay for the prospect. In a pretest, participants associated “risk and uncertainty” more with “lottery ticket” than with “gift card”, suggesting that even though the objective risk and uncertainty associated with the prospect in the two conditions were identical, simply framing a prospect as a “lottery ticket” increased the perceived risk associated with that prospect (relative to an “gift card”). This claim was tested using an online between-subjects experiment (Amazon Mechanical Turk participants). Participants indicated their willingness to pay for a risky prospect that was framed as either a “lottery ticket” or an “gift card”. In the lottery condition, the “lottery ticket” would for sure yield either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). In the gift card condition, the “gift card” would be either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). Participants in both conditions were also told that the researchers would randomly select five respondents from all survey respondents to get a $20 bonus. For each of the five selected respondent, if their willingness to pay for either the lottery ticket or the gift card was above the researchers’ reservation price (the reservation price of $15 was not revealed to participants), they would buy the lottery ticket or the gift card at the authors’ reservation price. If their willingness to pay was below the reservation price, they would not buy the lottery ticket or gift card. Furthermore, participants were not told how many other participants completed the survey, so they were unaware of the probability of being selected to receive the bonus. To detect participants who did not pay attention to the instructions, the authors administered an instructional manipulation check (Oppenheimer, Meyvis, and Davidenko 2009) at the beginning of the experiment. Participants could start the experiment only after they had correctly answered the instructional manipulation check. Finally, to check whether participants erroneously believed that $0 was a possible payoff, participants were asked, “What was the lowest possible outcome of the offer?” and chose an answer from the values $0, $5, $10, $15, and $20 (Simonsohn, 2009). The authors analyzed and compared willingness to pay with a t-test (Yang et al., 2013, p.726): “Participants in the lottery condition were willing to pay less (M = $5.68, SD = $6.69, Mdn = $5.00) than participants in the uncertain gift card condition (M = $9.52, SD = $4.48, Mdn = $ 7.50; t(99) = 3.43, p < .001, ηp2 = .11; z = 2.93, p = .003).” The present study will replicate this claim, which has been selected for the SCORE program.
