title_r: Pastotter_Cognition_2013_EQxa - Berry_6738 - Direct Replication
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Pastötter et al (2013) is that positive moods validate thoughts about pushing in the active decision frame (“yes, it is appropriate to push”) and validate thoughts about not pushing in the passive decision frame (“yes, it is not appropriate to push”), inducing utilitarian responding in the active frame and non utilitarian responding in the passive frame. In contrast, negative moods invalidate thoughts about pushing in the active decision frame (“no, it is not appropriate to push”) and invalidate thoughts about not pushing in the passive decision frame (“no, it is not appropriate to not push”), inducing non utilitarian responding in the active frame and utilitarian responding in the passive frame. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Compared to neutral moods, positive moods induced utilitarian responding (i.e., deciding to push) in the active decision frame, but induced non utilitarian responding (i.e., deciding to not push) in the passive decision frame; in negative moods, exactly the opposite picture arose.” Participants’ yes/no responses to the dilemma in Experiment 1 were analyzed using an F test with the between-subjects factors of mood (positive, negative) and frame (active, passive). The factor mood was manipulated by presenting different musical selections to induce positive (happy) and negative (sad) moods. The factor frame was manipulated by asking participants different closing questions after presentation of the footbridge scenario. This analysis yielded that affective influences on moral judgment varied with decision frame, F(1, 396) = 29.0, p < .001, partial eta squared = .07. The aim of this study is to replicate the claims made by Pastötter et al. (2013) about positive and negative moods on utilitarian responses. First, we will attempt to replicate that positive moods induce utilitarian responding in the active decision frame, but induce non-utilitarian responding in the passive decision frame. Second, we will attempt to replicate the claim that negative moods induce non-utilitarian responding in the active decision frame and utilitarian responding in the passive decision frame.

title_r: Is There a Positive Association between Working Memory Capacity and Mind Wandering in a Low-Demand Breathing Task? A Preregistered Replication of Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012)
abstract_r: Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012, Experiment 2) found that working memory capacity (WMC) correlated positively with mind-wandering propensity measured by thought probes in a breath-monitoring task, but was unassociated with the tendency to self-catch mind-wandering. Here, I sought to replicate the associations between mind-wandering and WMC in the Levinson et al. breath task. With data from a large sample of subjects and two measures of WMC, the data from the current study suggests that, if WMC correlates with probe-caught mind wandering, it is most likely negative. In addition, the evidence regarding self-caught mind wandering is consistent with Levinson et al. for the sum of self-caught responses, but when self-caught responses are considered in proportion to probe-caught mind wandering, modest evidence was found for a positive association with WMC.

title_r: Affect labelling with words and emojis: a replication and extension of Vlasenko, Rogers and Waugh (2021)
abstract_r: A body of previous literature mostly gives the message that affect labelling downregulates negative emotions, and many of the proposed mechanisms are in line with distancing-related processes. For instance, the distraction account suggests affect labelling reduces negative emotions because the task itself diverts people’s attention away from the aversive stimuli (images/videos in most cases); the symbolic conversion account indicates that it is the conversion between information modalities (from images to language mostly) that helps create psychological distancing from the original stimuli and reduces its emotional impact. Nevertheless, in the series of studies conducted by Vlasenko, Rogers and Waugh (2021), affect labelling has been found to consistently increase positive emotion intensity but showed no effect on negative emotions. Similarly, Xi and Vinson (2022 & 2023, in preparation) found that affect labelling enhanced positive emotional responses to positively-valenced sentences (thus, a situation in which symbolic conversion did not take place) but the effect on negative emotions appeared unstable. In addition, Xi and Vinson (2023, in preparation) included a condition in which participants were asked to use emojis, rather than words for affect labelling. Effects of emoji labelling (putting feelings into emojis) did not differ from the traditional affect labelling task (emotion word labelling/putting feelings into words) in terms of their effects on emotion intensity. These findings together challenge the symbolic conversion account: in these studies affect labelling influenced emotional responses whether there was symbolic conversion or not, and this opposite direction of effect (increased emotions for positive stimuli) does not align with the distancing process as indicated by distraction or symbolic conversion accounts. In order to gain a better understanding of the effects and mechanisms of affect labelling, and to fully test the symbolic conversion account, we need to test whether effects of affect labelling can be observed in circumstances where conversion does not take place, and linguistic labels are not used: affect labelling for image stimuli, using emotional emojis instead of words. To do this, our first step is to replicate Vlasenko, Rogers and Waugh (2021) (Experiment 1) with timing modifications as in Xi & Vinson (2023, in prep) and additionally testing whether the same pattern persists when we compare the effects of emotion word labelling and emoji labelling on emotional responses to affective images (Experiment 2), before we firmly reject the symbolic conversion account. We also take into consideration the individual difference factor of trait worry in both Experiments to better understand how labelling affects emotion-related processes.

title_r: Ambivalence of Neutral Ratings: A conceptual Replication of Anvari et al. (2023) Regarding Affective Norms for German Sentiment Terms Using Different Response Formats
abstract_r: Our study is based on the work of Anvari, Bachmann, Sanchez-Burks, and Schneider (2023). They examine the Affective Norms for English Words (ANEW) (Bradley, M. M., & Lang, P. J., 1999; 2010) database and, in particular, the question of whether words that are classified as 'neutral' on a bipolar valence scale can actually in some cases be ambivalent. The ANEW provides normative ratings for English words on bipolar scales of valence (emotional positivity vs. negativity) and arousal (degree of activation or deactivation) and is often used in psychological studies to select stimuli that elicit specific affective responses. Valence measures how positive or negative a word feels, while arousal measures how stimulating or calming it is. "Neutral" words tend to fall in the middle of a bipolar valence scale, which theoretically indicates a lack of positive or negative emotional activation. The ambivalent nature of words can be reflected in a neutral response on a valence scale when the answer represents a compromise between positive and negative emotional states. However, the distinction between true neutrality and ambivalence is crucial in emotion research. True neutrality implies the absence of emotional responses, while ambivalence involves the simultaneous experience of both positive and negative reactions. This distinction is important for studies that aim to use "neutral" stimuli as a baseline for non-emotional responses, as ambivalent words may introduce confounding emotional elements. Anvari et al. (2023) employed three methods to assess ambivalence: subjective ambivalence ratings, objective ambivalence calculated using a specific formula, and the minimum statistic (MIN stat), which represents the lower of two ratings given on two unipolar scales for the positivity and negativity of a stimulus. A higher MIN stat score indicates a greater intensity of ambivalence, as this method objectively captures ambivalence by emphasizing the lesser of the positive and negative ratings, thereby reducing the risk of one emotional response overshadowing the other. This approach differs from the conventional 9-point valence scale, which typically assesses emotional polarity on a bipolar rather than a unipolar scale. Additionally, Anvari et al. (2023) employed the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) scale to assess valence and arousal. The SAM scale is a visual representation of a 9-point scale comprising human-like figures in various emotional states. Valence is evaluated on a bipolar scale, with a value of 1 indicating negative affect and a value of 9 indicating positive affect. In contrast, arousal is measured on a unipolar scale, with a value of 1 indicating low arousal and a value of 9 indicating high arousal. The SAM scale is particularly effective for capturing affective dimensions due to its simple, non-verbal format, which allows participants to rate their emotional responses in an intuitive, visually guided manner. Since we are aiming for a conceptual replication of this study, we adapted our methodology to include alternative response formats for measuring valence. Specifically, we measured valence using two different response formats: the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and the Dual Range Slider (DRS). We want to find out whether the results of Anvari et al. (2023) can be replicated with the conceptually similar VAS and whether replication can also be achieved with the conceptually more distant DRS. The introduction of VAS and DRS allows us to investigate whether these formats can capture similar nuances in valence and ambivalence as the SAM scale used by Anvari et al. (2023). The Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) involves rating the word on two scales, one ranging from neutral (0) to positive (100) and the other from neutral (0) to negative (-100), with the slider starting at the middle (50) which can be moved to the desired position on each scale. Depending on the position of the slider the resulting value can be between 0 and 100 or -100. This setup enables us to calculate the MIN stat similar to Anvari et al. (2023) from these ratings, which provides an objective measure of ambivalence based on the participants’ ratings on both the positive and negative dimensions. The Dual Range Slider (DRS) differs from the VAS in that it measures valence on a single bipolar scale with two sliders, allowing participants to indicate a range of emotional responses from negative to positive. This produces a range rather than a single value, potentially offering a broader depiction of the participant’s valence response and an alternative approach to assessing ambivalence, by looking at the width of the slider. The DRS allows both negative and positive values to be expressed simultaneously and could therefore overcome the problem of the bipolar scale used by Anvari et al. (2023), where this is not possible. In assessing arousal, we followed the approach of Anvari et al. (2023). We measured arousal using the 9-point Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) scale, with the verbal anchors “calm” (“ruhig”) and “exciting” (“aufgeregt”) provided only in the explanation of the example item. The use of the SAM scale for arousal in both studies ensures consistency in measuring this dimension, which allows for a more direct comparison between the studies. Anvari et al. (2023) selected 60 neutral words from the ANEW database, with valence scores ranging from 4.95 to 5.05 on a 9-point scale. Since our study is conducted in Germany, we used the BAWL-R database (Võ et al., 2009) for German words. We selected 40 neutral words ranging from -0.5 to 0.5 on a 7-point valence scale (-3 to 3), with 20 neutral words rated as high arousal and 20 rated as low arousal. Additionally, we selected 20 negative and 20 positive words as reference points, resulting in a total of 80 words. These selection criteria allowed us to approximate the valence range used by Anvari et al. (2023) within the BAWL-R’s framework, ensuring that our “neutral” stimuli meet comparable criteria for neutrality and arousal in a German-language context. In summary, our study builds upon Anvari et al. (2023) by examining if the valence and arousal ratings of words can be replicated using alternative response formats and a German language database. This approach serves not only to test the robustness of the results presented by Anvari et al., but also to extend their findings by introducing response formats that may capture finer emotional nuances. The use of a single bipolar interval response scale to assess ambivalence could contribute to the broader field of emotion measurement.

title_r: Re‑examining the effect of wage delegation : a replication study of Charness et al. (2012)
abstract_r: Experimental research has explored the effects of wage delegation on employee performance, with the pioneering attempt by (Charness et al., Am Econ Rev 102:2358–2379, 2012) in “The Hidden Advantage of Delegation: Pareto Improvements in a Gift Exchange Game”, published in the American Economic Review. We conducted a replication of their experiment for two main reasons: first, to validate the original findings that have influenced subsequent research, and second, to examine whether these results hold in contexts with reduced social proximity between workers and employers, a relevant issue due to the rise of remote work. Our online experiment, involving 410 participants, followed the original study’s design but used a different sample. We successfully replicated the main finding that wage delegation increases employee effort, though the effect was smaller and largely due to employees granting themselves higher wages. These results support the notion that with decreasing social proximity, formal controls increase in importance.

title_r: Do Stereotypes Simplify Cognitive Processing? Examining The Cognitive Toolbox Through A Replication And Extension Of Macrae et al. (1994)
abstract_r: Stereotyping occurs in a wide variety of situations and can have severe and negative consequences. One potential explanation for the function of stereotypes offered by Macrae et al. (1994) is that they allow easier mental categorization of individuals and alleviate cognitive load. This can result in more attention for other tasks. In this thesis, I replicated Macrae et al.’s (1994) Study 1 using similar materials and procedures, while also addressing potential limitations to their research. Macrae et al. (1994) found that providing stereotype labels facilitated performance on a secondary task. In my replication study, I found no such facilitation effects. Further research needs to be done to fully understand the relationship between stereotyping and its potential to relieve cognitive load, but my study casts doubt on the reliability of Macrae et al.’s (1994) findings.

title_r: Giving and taking in dictator games – differences by gender? A replication study of Chowdhury et al. (Southern Economic Journal, 2017)

(Southern Economic Journal, 2017)" by Korbinian von Blanckenburg, Eva Tebbe, and Anja Iseke, published in: Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, Volume 2, 2023-1. Abstract: This study attempts to replicate experimental results from Chowdhury et al. published in Southern Economic Journal (2017). They study gender differences in the giving and taking variants of the dictator game. Using the same experimental design on a sample of German students our findings differ from Chowdhury et al. (2017). In contrast to the original study, we do not find support for an asymmetric gender effect. Our results indicate that, on average, both men and women allocate similar amounts in the giving and in the taking frame. Aditional analyses indicate that men are more likely than women to allocate nothing in the taking variant rather than in the giving variant, in line with Chowdhury et al. (2017).

title_r: Historical Communist Party Strength and Modern Party Loyalty. A Replication Study of Barceló (PNAS, 2021)
abstract_r: Replication data for “The Long-term Effects of War Exposure on Civic Engagement,” published September 2021, and “Corrections for Barceló, The Long-term Effects of War Exposure on Civic Engagement,” published online July 2023 and February 2024, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The corrections purport to address several issues in a 2021 publication, which we raised with both PNAS and the author. As we describe in our replication study, the corrections are themselves flawed and continue to lead to misleading findings. Barceló commits three major errors that render his research design inappropriate and his conclusions problematic. First, Barceló again commits a critical coding error that again leads him to attest incorrectly that he is clustering standard errors (SEs) at the provincial level, when in fact he is only using robust SEs, leading to false assertions of statistical significance and instrument strength. title_r: LeBoeuf_JournMarketRes_2010_EKBZ - Yoon - Direct Replication - 618k
abstract_r: LeBoeuf & Simmons (2010) has shown that products predominantly associated with utilitarian attitudes at the category level support less utilitarian and more symbolic attitudes at the brand level and products predominantly associated with symbolic attitudes at the category level support less symbolic and more utilitarian attitudes at the brand level. The current research aims to test the robustness and replicability of this finding with a larger new sample. The claim selected from LeBoeuf et al. (2010) is that products predominantly associated with utilitarian attitudes at the category level support less utilitarian and more symbolic attitudes at the brand level. Products predominantly associated with symbolic attitudes at the category level support less symbolic and more utilitarian attitudes at the brand level (H1). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: “Specifically, product categories that are generally associated with utilitarian attitudes are associated with less utilitarian, more symbolic attitudes when branded, whereas product categories that are generally associated with symbolic attitudes are associated with more utilitarian, less symbolic attitudes when branded.” To test the claim, participants evaluated eight products (four utilitarian products and four symbolic products), with product order counterbalanced and symbolic and utilitarian products intermixed. The authors randomly assigned participants to evaluate branded or unbranded products, and they further randomly assigned those evaluating branded products to one of two sets of brand names. Participants rated each product’s associations with symbols and benefits, and the authors obtain difference scores by subtracting each product’s symbolism rating from its benefits rating, revealing the degree to which each product supports, on balance, more utilitarian (higher numbers) or more symbolic (lower numbers) attitudes. The authors perform a 2 (level: category or brand) × 2 (unbranded product type: utilitarian or symbolic) mixed ANOVA on the difference scores (averaged for each product type). A 2 (level: category or brand) × 2 (unbranded product type: utilitarian or symbolic) mixed ANOVA on the difference scores (averaged for each product type) revealed the predicted level × product type interaction (F(1, 204) = 7.70, p = 0.006).

title_r: Virtual tool embodiment: A replication and extension of Cardinali et al. (2009) in a virtual environment
abstract_r: Recently, it has been suggested that movements in virtual environments may leverage different mechanisms than those in real environments, making it essential to validate virtual reality for the study of motor control and related processes, such as tool-use (Harris et al., 2019). A predominant theory of tool-use, termed tool embodiment, posits that tool-use is facilitated by changes to a highly plastic, action-oriented body representation termed the body schema (Martel, Cardinali, Roy, & Farnè, 2016). Following seminal work by Cardinali et al. (2009), changes in reaching kinematics and participants' localization of body landmarks have been taken as an indicators of tool embodiment. To determine whether the use of a virtual environment influences these tool-use effects, the present study seeks to replicate Cardinali et al. (2009)'s original work with several extensions, including the projection of a virtual environment via head-mounted display. Additionally, this work aims to clarify questions which remain unanswered by the literature substantiating the tool embodiment perspective. For example, it is unclear whether measures of the body representation are valid for their purpose: Kinematics have no clear relationship with the properties of the arm said to be altered by tool-use. Further, there are no instances wherein two tool embodiment measures have been successfully correlated within the same sample of participants.

title_r: Direct Replication of Bago et al. (2023)
abstract_r: This study aims to conduct a direct replication of Bago et al. (2023), whose results challenge the Motivated System 2 Reasoning (MS2R) hypothesis (Kahan, 2013), which posits that analytical processing (Kahneman, 2011) strengthens motivated reasoning, particularly ideological. Using a two-response paradigm (an intuitive response followed by a deliberative one), Bago et al. (2023) showed that deliberation increases the consistency between individuals’ evaluations of climate change information and their prior factual beliefs, rather than with their political ideology. The goal of the present study is to replicate these findings while introducing several methodological improvements: (1) conducting power analyses based on the original study’s results to determine the most appropriate sample size; (2) controlling for participants’ prior beliefs at recruitment — by selecting only individuals who believe in climate change — in order to reduce inter-individual differences in our sample and minimize statistical noise that could affect the validity of the results; (3) implementing methodological improvements to the original study materials. Participants will be divided into two groups, each evaluating six vignettes adapted from Bago et al. (2023), presenting arguments either in favor of or against the existence of climate change or its human origin. In the experimental group, participants will follow a two-response paradigm: after completing a cognitive load task (Dot Memory Task; Miyake et al., 2001), they will first evaluate each vignette under time pressure (intuitive processing), then a second time without time constraints (analytical processing). The control group will evaluate the same vignettes only once, without time constraints or cognitive load. Replicating the approach of Bago et al. (2023), and consistent with their results, we expect that compared to intuitive processing, participants in the control condition (one response condition) are expected to be more influenced by their prior beliefs. We expect an interaction effect, such that participants in the control condition will show more agreement with arguments supporting (PRO) the existence of climate change than participants in the intuitive processing condition. Conversely, agreement with arguments opposing (CON) the existence of climate change is expected to be lower under the control condition than under intuitive processing. This interaction is expected regardless of participants' political ideology. On an exploratory basis, we will also perform a comparison between the intuitive and analytical processing conditions in the two-response paradigm group. We expect the same pattern as the previous hypothesis: Participants in the analytical processing condition will show more agreement with arguments supporting (PRO) the existence of climate change than participants in the intuitive processing condition. Conversely, agreement with arguments opposing (CON) the existence of climate change is expected to be lower under analytical processing than under intuitive processing. This interaction is expected regardless of participants' political ideology. These latter analyses will be conducted in an exploratory way, as it is possible that we observe an anchoring effect (as previously found by Bago et al. (2023)) of the initial response on the final response, thus reducing the magnitude of our interaction. This anchoring can be assessed by comparing final responses to those of a control group providing only a single response.

title_r: Socio-Affective Processes of Narcissism in Daily Life: A Pre-registered Replication and Extension of Wright et al. 2017
abstract_r: Narcissism is associated with significant interpersonal problems (e.g., Campbell et al., 2005; Ogrodniczuk et al., 2009; Pincus et al., 2009). To understand specific triggers for narcissistic expression and potential mechanisms that generate interpersonal dysfunction, examining how individual differences in narcissism manifest in momentary interpersonal processes is necessary. However, despite much evidence that narcissism is associated with negative interpersonal outcomes (e.g., Miller et al., 2007), to date there are a limited number of studies that explicitly explore how narcissism contributes to momentary interpersonal processes. Recently, Wright and colleagues (2017) examined how narcissism amplifies links between interpersonal perceptions and one’s own behavior during social interactions in naturalistic settings. In particular, the authors explored how narcissism amplified the link between perceptions of others' dominance, negative affect, and one’s own quarrelsomeness (or low affiliation). Results revealed that others’ dominance did not predict one’s own dominant behavior in the interaction, but was associated with quarrelsome behavior. Negative affect was additionally found to account for the association of perceptions of others’ dominance and one’s own quarrelsome behavior. Further, it was identified that narcissism amplified the link between perceptions of others’ dominance and one’s own quarrelsomeness, as well as the link between others’ dominance and negative affect. These findings suggest that narcissism has important associations with momentary interpersonal and affective processes. Specifically, that perceptions of others’ dominance lead to negative affect and quarrelsomeness, especially for those high in narcissism. The present study serves as a replication of Wright and colleagues (2017). In particular, we aim to re-examine associations between momentary affective and interpersonal processes and whether narcissism amplifies these linkages. The current study extends Wright and colleagues (2017) by testing whether these effects are robust to sampling and assessment. We will explore these associations in a large community sample, oversampled for low modesty, a trait that is associated with narcissism. The original sample was a clinical sample with high levels of psychopathology. Whereas Wright and colleagues (2017) used diagnostic interviews to measure narcissism (and personality pathology more broadly), here we use contemporary narcissism measures that can be scored for grandiose and vulnerable features, as well as the three-factor structure of narcissism (e.g., Krizan & Herlache, 2018; Miller et al., 2017; Wright & Edershile, 2018). This is an important extension as there are likely differential effects of grandiosity and vulnerability, as well as exhibitionistic grandiosity, entitlement, and vulnerability. Teasing apart which components of narcissism are primarily responsible for moderation effects is an important extension of Wright and colleagues (2017). Given established connections between grandiosity and dominance (e.g., Johnson et al., 2012), it is possible that grandiosity moderates the association between perceived dominance and one’s own warmth. However, vulnerability is associated with dysregulation (e.g., Edershile et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2018). Therefore, it is also possible that the narcissistic response is driven primarily by vulnerability. The inclusion of a three-factor structure will also help to further elucidate these findings, as it may be entitlement that primarily drives associations.

title_r: Disgust and the rubber hand illusion: A registered replication report of Jalal, Krishnakumar, and Ramachandran (2015)
abstract_r: Heightened experience of disgust is a feature of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), particularly in contamination-related OCD (C-OCD). Previous studies of the rubber hand illusion (RHI) reported that the sense of body ownership is related to the interaction between vision, touch, and proprioception. A recent study demonstrated a link between the RHI and disgust, reporting an interaction between these three perceptual modalities and disgust (Jalal, Krishnakumar, Ramachandran, 2015). However, there have been no direct replications of this initial study. We proposed a direct replication of Jalal et al.’s (2015) study. Based on a power analysis, we examined a minimum of 119 participants to determine whether placing contamination-related stimuli on a rubber hand causes OCD-like disgust among healthy participants while experiencing the RHI. In addition, we tested the cross-cultural validity of the previous findings, testing whether Japanese participants experience more intense disgust when a rubber hand and a participant’s hidden hand were stroked synchronously, compared with asynchronous stroking. This replication provides insight into potential applications of this study protocol in the treatment of OCD.

title_r: Temporal Framing for Pro-Environmental Attitudes: Replications and Extensions of Baldwin & Lammers (2016)
abstract_r: More conservative people are more likely to reject climate protection policies than more liberal people (Bateman & O'Connor, 2016). As Climate protection gets more and more important, it is crucial to find a way to communicate climate change issues and solutions to appeal for conservatives (Baldwin & Lammers, 2016). In their study, Baldwin & Lammers (2016) theorized that the groups might prefer different temporal comparisons for many different reasons, for example because conservatives tend to compare the present with the past and liberals tend to compare the present with the future. Since appeals for climate protection measures are often formulated in terms of the future, they are probably not convincing for conservatives (Baldwin & Lammers, 2016). The idea is to provide the appeals with a past-related comparison (ibid.). In the studies by Baldwin & Lammers (2016), past-related comparisons led to stronger pro-environmental attitudes and more pro-environmental behavior among more conservative individuals. However, the current study situation is mixed: in some cases the effect could not be replicated (Kim et al., 2021; Stanley et al., 2021), in others it could (Herberz et al., 2023). The aim of the planned study is to investigate this effect again by also extending their work and adding a present frame to the past and the future frame. It will investigate whether conservatives show stronger pro-environmental approval of a text and stronger support for an environmental protection measure when it is formulated in terms of the past or present compared to a future-oriented formulation. This is also the outcome we expect. In addition, it will be investigated whether this effect is mediated by the psychological perception of distance and whether a past- or present-oriented frame reduces the perceived temporal and hypothetical distance of climate change among conservatives compared to a future-oriented frame. Here we assume that psychological distance only has an effect on conservatives, since liberals' pro-evironmental attitudes tend to be less influenced by framing.

title_r: Direct replication of a research claim from Goerg et al. (2010), in Journal of Labor Economics
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Goerg et al. (2010) is that the discriminating reward scheme under the production function of complementarity achieves almost maximum efficiency, whereas it leads to significantly lower efficiency rates under the production function of substitutability. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Our experimental results demonstrate that unequal rewards can potentially increase productivity by facilitating coordination and that the effect strongly interacts with the exact shape of the production function." The study implements an experiment where three players work on a joint project and exert costly efforts. Their total sum of effort determines the number of some goods produced by the joint project for a given production function. The payoff of a player is given by productivity (i.e., the number of produced goods) multiplied by an individual reward, minus the cost of effort. The authors create four different treatments by manipulating the characteristics of the production function (either a function of complementarity or of substitutability) as well as of the reward scheme (either a symmetrical or a discriminating mechanism). The evidence for the finding used by the SCORE program comes from a comparison, with a rank-sum test, of the mean effort level in rounds 1-5 between the 345COM and 345SUB conditions, which are both subject to the discriminating treatment. Focusing on the discriminating reward scheme, overall effort levels are significantly higher (p = .0004, two-tailed) under a production function of complementarity than under a production function of substitutability: 91.7% of all effort decisions in 345COM are to work hard, compared to only 65.3% in treatment 345SUB.

title_r: Human Capital Theory and Venture Capital Firms: Exploring ‘‘Home runs’’ and ‘‘Strike Outs’’ – A Replication and Extension of Dimov and Shepherd (2005)
abstract_r: The present work is a registered report focused on a replication and extension of the findings in Dimov and Shepherd (2005). Our work tests the hypotheses from the original article in an expanded industry context and with an updated sample. The wider sample will include low- and medium-tech industries, and an expanded time frame as opposed to the original sample based on the high-tech wireless industry in a 5-year span. We will test using the same estimation technique (hierarchical regression) from the original article and expand on it by using multivariate regression and negative binomial analyses to accommodate the count nature of the outcome variables. We expect that this extension will support the finding that general human capital has a significant effect on success (home-runs) measured through Initial Public Offerings (IPOs). Furthermore, we anticipate that findings will support predicted inferences regarding the relations among general and specific human capital with failures (strike-outs) measured through bankruptcies. Our replication efforts are crucial in examining 1) whether lower technological industries require similar quality human capital, or if high-tech industries demand more; 2) if we can invest in individual level human capital to benefit firm level performance; and 3) if lower technology industries also require other forms of highly specialized human capital. Overall, we anticipate that this replication and extension can facilitate continued, nuanced, research in this area.

title_r: Does approximate numeracy predict superior decision making beyond objective and subjective numeracy? Registered replication report on Schley and Peters (2014)
abstract_r: Everyday decision making requires dealing with numbers related to potential outcomes and their probabilities. A bulk of research from Judgement and Decision Making field (for a review see: Cokely et al., 2018; Garcia-Retamero, Sobkow, Petrova, Garrido, & Traczyk, 2019) showed that superior decision making is largely driven by individual differences in objective statistical numeracy—an ability to understand statistical and probability information and to use it in everyday contexts. Nevertheless, a few recent studies suggested that an ability to estimate quantities and to map symbolic numbers into mental number line may be an equally important predictor of decision making as objective numeracy. The aim of the present research is to replicate one of the first and most important studies showing this effect (study 2 from Schley & Peters, 2014; Psychological Science; more than 100 citations). In this study, 99 participants completed an adaptive decision task (a series of monetary gambles), enabling estimation of parameters from the Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Moreover, participants solved a number-line task to measure symbolic-number mapping (Siegler & Opfer, 2003), a set of mathematical tasks measuring objective numeracy (Weller et al., 2013) and answered few questions regarding demography (age, sex, income, education). The results of this study showed that participants with more exact symbolic-number mappings exhibited more linear value functions in a decision task. Moreover, more exact symbolic-number mapping mediated the relationship between objective numeracy and value-function parameters suggesting that this ability may (at least partially) explain the relationship between numeracy and decision making. In our research, we plan to extend this experimental procedure by including the Subjective Numeracy Scale (Fagerlin et al., 2007) as a measure of numeric confidence. This approach would allow us to test the replicability of the relationship between symbolic-number mapping and value function parameters as well as to compare the relative contribution of three types of numeric competencies: objective numeracy, approximate numeracy, and subjective numeracy proposed recently by Peters and Bjalkebring (2015).

title_r: Are STEM Faculty Biased Against Female Applicants? A Robust Replication and Extension of Moss-Racusin and Colleagues (2012)
abstract_r: Abstract (as of 6/1/20): In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through four studies--two direct replications, one extension, and a meta analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. The pre-registered data analysis plans will provide a strong test assessing the replicability of Moss-Racusin et al. (2012)’s finding that STEM faculty were biased against women who applied for a lab manager position.

title_r: Ulrich (1991) Replication and Extension
abstract_r: This study is a replication and extension of Ulrich (1991). We ask, to what extent is the restorative effect of nature on affective stress moderated by personality? Although data has been collected for this study, analyses have not yet been conducted. Data collection occurred between April 2018 and September 2018 at the University of Virginia. Data was collected as part of a multilab replication effort of Ulrich (1991) led by Dr. Tanja-Dijkstra, NL. For the current project, only the data collected at the University of Virginia will be analyzed (N = 84). Additionally, only a subset of the measures collected will be analyzed; our project is focused on measures of personality and psychological restoration (as captured by self-report scales of affective stress), and therefore excludes physiological data collected). Details of the multilab replication effort can be found at https://osf.io/ygjw9.

title_r: Revisiting Nature, Spirituality, and Well-being: a post-Covid-19 replication study of Kamitsis and Francis (2013)
abstract_r: The aim of the present study is to investigate the relationships between nature connectedness, exposure to nature, spirituality, and psychological well-being by replicating the methods used in Kamitsis and Francis (2013). Kamitsis and Francis (2013) suggested that exposure and connectedness to nature were positively associated with well-being and increased spirituality. They also noted that their participants’ spirituality may be the reason for the positive effects nature had on their well-being. Similar to Kamitsis and Francis (2013), the present study hypothesises that exposure and connectedness to nature will be positively associated with psychological well-being and spirituality. It is also predicted that the relationship of nature exposure and nature connectedness with psychological well-being will be mediated by spirituality.

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r: The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”. We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals reduces the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” where Y is replaced with a common Muslim name compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. We expect reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased.

title_r: Does the Corollary Discharge Provide the Sensory Content of Inner Speech? A Preregistered Direct Replication and Extension of Scott (2013)
abstract_r: The mental production of speech or "inner speech" is a remarkable and foundational ability in humans, involved in many daily activities such as reading, writing, remembering, or planning. Inner speech is generally accompanied by a subjective multisensory (mainly auditory) experience. However, the cognitive processes leading to these sensory percepts remain poorly known. One prominent perspective is that the sensory content of inner speech would correspond to the predicted sensory consequences of inhibited speech acts. Scott (2013) provided experimental evidence suggesting that inner speech indeed involves the mental simulation of speech acts, as evidenced by the attenuation of the effect of an external sound. However, Scott (2013) assessed silent speech, but not inner speech, which in contrast to silent speech, does not involve visible articulatory movements. The present work aims to replicate and extend the study of Scott (2013) to assess whether inner speech attenuates the perception of concomitant external speech sounds.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

title_r: Experiment 1 - Replicating and extending Summers et al. (2021)
abstract_r: This study is part of a research project aiming to explore pain perception biases in different contexts (including physical, psychological and social pain), in turn seeking to better understand and address the factors that contribute to the health disparities faced by neurodivergent populations. Therefore, the project investigates potential biases in the perception of pain when experienced by neurodivergent individuals, and explores how these biases contribute to health disparities. Previous research has identified health disparities between neurodivergent and non-neurodivergent populations, such as higher premature mortality in individuals with ADHD and autism. These differences may stem in part from differences in access to health care services, which may be influenced by implicit biases in others' pain perception. Therefore this first experiment aims to determine whether a bias exists in judgements about physical pain when the person experiencing the pain is neurodivergent. We will test whether there is a bias in the judgement of pain by neurodivergent individuals relative to non-neurodivergent individuals through the description of painful events.

title_r: Bartels_JournConsRes_2015_mrZ - Chandler_579 - Direct Replication
abstract_r: This study consists of two parts, a pilot study and a replication study. Pilot Study. To support the replication study, we will conduct a pilot test to identify a suitable product or product category to include in the study materials for this replication. A suitable product or product category is one that between 35% and 80% of people are willing to purchase. Replication Study. This study will replicate Study 1a of Bartels and Urminsky (2015), which found that cueing the opportunity cost potentiates the relationship between connectedness to the future self and choosing not to spend money. The relationship between caring about the future outcomes (as measured by the average of the two connectedness to the future self items) and choosing to save (as opposed to purchase) is only present when participants are reminded of the opportunity costs of purchasing. This reflects the following claim from the paper's abstract: “[C]ues that highlight opportunity costs reduce spending primarily when people …are more connected to their future selves.” The claim is tested by assessing the significance of the difference between two correlation coefficients using a z-test: correlation between an index of participants’ measured connection to future self and a dichotomous choice to spend or not spend money when opportunity cost is highlighted (point-biserial correlation r(43) = 0.41), versus the correlation between the connectedness measure and the dichotomous choice when opportunity cost is not highlighted (point-biserial correlation (r(45) = 0.04). This yielded a significant difference between correlation coefficients, z = 2.14, p < 0.05.

In addition, we have developed further hypotheses that relate to the differentiated consideration of the construct BJW in personal belief in a just world (PBJW) and general belief in a just world (GBJW) measured with the scales of Dalbert (1999). Concretely, we predict the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 1a: Participants high in BJW will be more likely to collect the gift. Hypothesis 1b: PBJW will show a stronger positive correlation with gift collection than GBJW. Hypothesis 2a: BJW will be positively correlated with general trust. title_r: The Possible Unemployment Cost of Average Inflation Below a Credible Target. A Replication Study of Svensson (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2015)
abstract_r: This paper replicates the main analysis of Svensson (2015) with some expansion to the original analysis, mainly for the United States. Overall, the replication exercise successfully confirms the conclusions of Svensson (2015). In both Sweden and the United States, empirical evidence sup- ports the existence of a non-vertical long run Phillips curve. The slope of the long run Phillips curve recorded -0.75 in Sweden and -0.23 in the United States. While the average inflation rate in the United States was very close to its targeted level, the average inflation rate in Sweden was 0.6 per- centage points below its targeted level over the sample period. The deviation of inflation rate from its targeted level in Sweden resulted in an unemployment cost equivalent to 0.8 percentage points over the sample period where the average unemployment rate recorded 7.4 percent compared with an estimated 6.6 percent had the average inflation rate been at its targeted level.

title_r: The positive-negative mode link between brain connectivity, demographics, and behavior: A pre-registered replication of Smith et al. 2015
abstract_r: In mental health research, it has proven difficult to find measures of brain function that provide reliable indicators of mental health and well-being, including susceptibility to mental health disorders. Recently, a family of data-driven analyses have provided such reliable measures when applied to large, population-level datasets. In the current pre-registered replication study, we show that the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) methods previously developed using resting-state MRI functional connectivity and subject measures of cognition and behavior from healthy adults are also effective in measuring well-being (a "positive-negative axis") in an independent developmental dataset. Our replication was successful in two out of three of our pre-registered criteria, such that a primary CCA mode's weights displayed a significant positive relationship and explained a significant amount of variance in both functional connectivity and subject measures. The only criteria that was not successful was that compared to other modes the magnitude of variance explained by the primary CCA mode was smaller than predicted, a result which could indicate a developmental trajectory of a primary mode. This replication establishes a signature neurotypical relationship between connectivity and phenotype, opening new avenues of research in neuroscience with clear clinical applications.

title_r: Reproduction Package for FSE 2024 Submission `A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification'
abstract_r:
Reproduction Package A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification Abstract This artifact is a reproduction package for the manuscript “A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification”, submitted to FSE 2024. In the replication study, the transferability of the results reported by two prior publications on interpolation-based hardware model checking to software verification is investigated. The two publications are (1) Interpolation-Sequence-Based Model Checking (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009) and (2) Intertwined Forward-Backward Reachability Analysis Using Interpolants (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). The purpose of this artifact is to reproduce the experiments conducted to validate the claims made in the above two publications. The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the evaluation of the replication study, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code and binaries of CPAchecker (at revision 44757 of branch “cfa-single-loop-transformation”), which implements the verification algorithms compared in the submitted manuscript, the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark suite, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments. This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The VM has all the required dependencies installed. If you test this artifact with it, all installation steps below can be skipped. Contents This artifact contains the following items: README.*: this documentation fse2024-paper483.pdf: the manuscript submitted to FSE 2024 License.txt: license information of the artifact cpachecker/: a directory containing the source code and precompiled binaries of CPAchecker sv-benchmarks/: a directory containing the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark tasks used in our evaluation data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data produced from our full evaluation (used in the manuscript, under paper-results/) and from a demo experiment (prepared for this reproduction package, under demo-results/) bench-defs/: a directory containing the benchmark and table definitions of the experiments (used by BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking) This readme file will guide you through the following steps: Execute CPAchecker Perform experiments View the experimental results Execute CPAchecker System requirements for CPAchecker To execute CPAchecker, Java Runtime Environment (JRE) version ≥ 17 is required. For more information, please refer to cpachecker/INSTALL.md. Run verification algorithms in CPAchecker In the replication study, we compared the performance of three interpolation-based verification algorithms, namely IMC (McMillan, 2003), ISMC (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009), and DAR (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). ISMC and DAR are the algorithms proposed by the two prior publications, respectively, and IMC is the first interpolation-based model-checking approach, which was used as the baseline in the two publications. All the algorithms have been implemented in CPAchecker. Below we list the commands to run the evaluated verification algorithms. These example commands use sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c as the input program. You can replace it with another program. IMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolation \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ -setprop imc.loopBoundIncrementStrategyForBMC=CONST \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
ISMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
DAR: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationDualSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop dar.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
For more information on how to run CPAchecker, see cpachcker/README.md. Understand the output of CPAchecker The following is an example output shown on the console after an analysis is finished. 
[...redacted...] Verification result: TRUE. No property violation found by chosen configuration. More details about the verification run can be found in the directory "./output". Graphical representation included in the file "./output/Report.html".
There are 3 possible outcomes of the verification result: TRUE: the program is “safe”, i.e., it satisfies the given safety property FALSE: the program is “unsafe”, i.e., it contains a violation to the given safety property UNKNOWN: the analysis was inconclusive CPAchecker also generates an HTML report for conveniently browsing the results. Please refer to cpachecker/doc/Report.md for more information. Perform Experiments Install BenchExec We use BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking and resource measurements, to perform our evaluation. Please follow the installation guide to set up the benchmarking environment. Experimental settings The settings are described in the XML file bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. This XML file is used by BenchExec for limiting computing resources and scheduling runs. For the execution of a task, a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 1800 seconds of CPU time, and 15 GB of memory is imposed. Run the Full Evaluation To run the full experiment over the 8813 benchmark tasks reported in the manuscript, execute the following command. 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/
Run Partial Evaluation The full evaluation requires roughly 6 months of CPA time on a 3.40 GHz core. To run the experiment on a subset of benchmark tasks, you could add -t <tasks_name> to the above command, where <task_name> refer to the task names defined in bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. For example: 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/ \ -t ReachSafety-BitVectors
If you want to adjust the imposed resource limit, the following options can be used: 
-T <cputime_limit> -M <mem_limit>
For more information about these flags, please refer to benchexec -h. View the Experimental Results Generate Tables After the execution of an experiment, you can generate an interactive HTML by table-generator. Simply run: 
table-generator -x bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml \ -f html --no-diff -o results
Note that if the experiment is only performed on a single task set (via -t <tasks_name>), you have to replace bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml by bench-defs/subset-slt-stats.xml. Results from Our Experiments The results (both raw and processed data) of the partial run (on ReachSafety-BitVectors) and the full run obtained by our machines are in folders data-submission/demo-results/ and data-submission/paper-results/, respectively. The generated HTML tables are named overall-slt-stats.table.html under each respective folder. In the replication study, there are eight hypotheses extracted from the two prior publications. We list them below to make this document more standalone. For details, please refer to the bundled manuscript. Claims in the ISMC Publication H1.A: ISMC is faster than IMC on tasks with property violation. H1.B: ISMC is faster than IMC when IMC finds a proof only at high unrolling bounds. H1.C: Overall, ISMC is faster than IMC (by 30 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H1.A also for software verification, but H1.B and H1.C did not hold. Claims in the DAR Publication H2.A: For DAR, the ratio between iterations using global strengthening to the total number of iterations is less than 0.5 in most tasks. H2.B: IMC finds a proof slower than DAR in many tasks even though it has a smaller convergence length. H2.C: DAR computes more interpolants than IMC. H2.D: DAR’s run-time is more sensitive to the sizes of interpolants than IMC. H2.E: Overall, DAR is faster than IMC (by 36 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H2.A and H2.C also for software verification, but H2.B, H2.D, and H2.E did not hold. In the replication study, the transferability of the results reported by two prior publications on interpolation-based hardware model checking to software verification is investigated. The two publications are (1) Interpolation-Sequence-Based Model Checking (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009) and (2) Intertwined Forward-Backward Reachability Analysis Using Interpolants (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). The purpose of this artifact is to reproduce the experiments conducted to validate the claims made in the above two publications. The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the evaluation of the replication study, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code and binaries of CPAchecker (at revision 44757 of branch “cfa-single-loop-transformation”), which implements the verification algorithms compared in the submitted manuscript, the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark suite, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments. This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The VM has all the required dependencies installed. If you test this artifact with it, all installation steps below can be skipped. Contents This artifact contains the following items: README.*: this documentation fse2024-paper483.pdf: the manuscript submitted to FSE 2024 License.txt: license information of the artifact cpachecker/: a directory containing the source code and precompiled binaries of CPAchecker sv-benchmarks/: a directory containing the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark tasks used in our evaluation data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data produced from our full evaluation (used in the manuscript, under paper-results/) and from a demo experiment (prepared for this reproduction package, under demo-results/) bench-defs/: a directory containing the benchmark and table definitions of the experiments (used by BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking) This readme file will guide you through the following steps: Execute CPAchecker Perform experiments View the experimental results Execute CPAchecker System requirements for CPAchecker To execute CPAchecker, Java Runtime Environment (JRE) version ≥ 17 is required. For more information, please refer to cpachecker/INSTALL.md. Run verification algorithms in CPAchecker In the replication study, we compared the performance of three interpolation-based verification algorithms, namely IMC (McMillan, 2003), ISMC (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009), and DAR (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). ISMC and DAR are the algorithms proposed by the two prior publications, respectively, and IMC is the first interpolation-based model-checking approach, which was used as the baseline in the two publications. All the algorithms have been implemented in CPAchecker. Below we list the commands to run the evaluated verification algorithms. These example commands use sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c as the input program. You can replace it with another program. IMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolation \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ -setprop imc.loopBoundIncrementStrategyForBMC=CONST \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
ISMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
DAR: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationDualSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop dar.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
For more information on how to run CPAchecker, see cpachcker/README.md. Understand the output of CPAchecker The following is an example output shown on the console after an analysis is finished. 
[...redacted...] Verification result: TRUE. No property violation found by chosen configuration. More details about the verification run can be found in the directory "./output". Graphical representation included in the file "./output/Report.html".
There are 3 possible outcomes of the verification result: TRUE: the program is “safe”, i.e., it satisfies the given safety property FALSE: the program is “unsafe”, i.e., it contains a violation to the given safety property UNKNOWN: the analysis was inconclusive CPAchecker also generates an HTML report for conveniently browsing the results. Please refer to cpachecker/doc/Report.md for more information. Perform Experiments Install BenchExec We use BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking and resource measurements, to perform our evaluation. Please follow the installation guide to set up the benchmarking environment. Experimental settings The settings are described in the XML file bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. This XML file is used by BenchExec for limiting computing resources and scheduling runs. For the execution of a task, a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 1800 seconds of CPU time, and 15 GB of memory is imposed. Run the Full Evaluation To run the full experiment over the 8813 benchmark tasks reported in the manuscript, execute the following command. 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/
Run Partial Evaluation The full evaluation requires roughly 6 months of CPA time on a 3.40 GHz core. To run the experiment on a subset of benchmark tasks, you could add -t <tasks_name> to the above command, where <task_name> refer to the task names defined in bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. For example: 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/ \ -t ReachSafety-BitVectors
If you want to adjust the imposed resource limit, the following options can be used: 
-T <cputime_limit> -M <mem_limit>
For more information about these flags, please refer to benchexec -h. View the Experimental Results Generate Tables After the execution of an experiment, you can generate an interactive HTML by table-generator. Simply run: 
table-generator -x bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml \ -f html --no-diff -o results
Note that if the experiment is only performed on a single task set (via -t <tasks_name>), you have to replace bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml by bench-defs/subset-slt-stats.xml. Results from Our Experiments The results (both raw and processed data) of the partial run (on ReachSafety-BitVectors) and the full run obtained by our machines are in folders data-submission/demo-results/ and data-submission/paper-results/, respectively. The generated HTML tables are named overall-slt-stats.table.html under each respective folder. In the replication study, there are eight hypotheses extracted from the two prior publications. We list them below to make this document more standalone. For details, please refer to the bundled manuscript. Claims in the ISMC Publication H1.A: ISMC is faster than IMC on tasks with property violation. H1.B: ISMC is faster than IMC when IMC finds a proof only at high unrolling bounds. H1.C: Overall, ISMC is faster than IMC (by 30 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H1.A also for software verification, but H1.B and H1.C did not hold. Claims in the DAR Publication H2.A: For DAR, the ratio between iterations using global strengthening to the total number of iterations is less than 0.5 in most tasks. H2.B: IMC finds a proof slower than DAR in many tasks even though it has a smaller convergence length. H2.C: DAR computes more interpolants than IMC. H2.D: DAR’s run-time is more sensitive to the sizes of interpolants than IMC. H2.E: Overall, DAR is faster than IMC (by 36 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H2.A and H2.C also for software verification, but H2.B, H2.D, and H2.E did not hold. title_r: Knowledge Transfers from Multinational to Domestic Firms: Evidence from Worker Mobility. A Replication Study of Poole (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2013)
abstract_r: These data access descriptions, code and log files explain the results presented in the paper "Knowledge Transfers from Multinational to Domestic Firms: Evidence from Worker Mobility. A Replication Study of Poole (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2013)" by Stefanie A. Haller, Eoin T. Flaherty and Ragnhild Balsvik, published in: Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, Volume 2, 2023-3. Abstract: This paper replicates Poole (2013) using comprehensive Norwegian and Irish register data. Our results largely confirm the evidence documented in Poole for Brazil which suggests that when workers leave multinationals and are rehired at domestic establishments, the wages of their new coworkers who have already been present in the establishment increase. However, unlike suggested in the original article there is little indication that these spillovers differ in a statistically significant way across various dimensions of heterogeneity for any of the three countries.

title_r: Does sequence learning engage the frontoparietal network in 8-month-old infants? A replication and extension of Baek et al. (2022)
abstract_r: Sequence learning is a critical ability which serves as the cornerstone for developing many other cognitive and motor skills (e.g., Säfström et al., 2014), and it appears early in life. For example, 3-month-olds were able to detect audiovisual sequences with 3 elements compared to 4 elements for 4-month-olds (Lewkowicz, 2008), and 11-month-olds were able to respond to spatially structured sequences (Kirkham et al., 2007). Considering the relatively immature brain structure and network connectivity in infants, exploring the underlying neural basis for this ability in early infancy can help with our understanding of the development and functional capability of responsible networks when compared with findings from adult studies. However, only few studies touched upon this and among which, Baek and colleagues (2022) found an attenuation of frontal, parietal, and occipital responses towards predictable and thus learnable sequences in 6-month-olds. This fNIRS finding corresponds to the reduced prediction error in the predictive coding model (Friston, 2005). Moreover, a significantly greater functional connectivity in the frontoparietal network during predictable sequences (PS) compared to unpredictable sequences (UPS) was revealed (Baek et al., 2022), suggesting the involvement of the frontoparietal network in sequence learning and its early functioning at 6 months. Despite the evidence in adult studies (e.g., Koban et al., 2019; Leong et al., 2017), it was the first study demonstrating the involvement of the frontoparietal network during sequence learning in infant brains. For the current study, we plan to carry out a replication of Baek et al (2022) on 8-month-olds to confirm the potential functional role the frontoparietal network plays during sequence learning on an additional group of infants at a slightly older age, providing more evidence for the neural underpinnings of this ability. Infants wear an fNIRS headgear (NIRx Sport, 48 channels) when presented with both PS and UPS conditions in a counterbalanced order across participants (i.e., PS first or UPS first). For the analysis, besides the univariate analysis comparing brain activations towards PS and UPS, the background functional connectivity approach, which regresses out synchronized task-evoked responses, will also be applied to examine interactions between regions during learning. We expect to replicate the attenuation effect in the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobe, as well as the effect of greater functional connectivity in the frontoparietal network during learning in 8-month-old infants.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Weissman et al. (2020, Experiment 2)
abstract_r: The congruency sequence effect (CSE) refers to a smaller congruency effect after incongruent trials than after congruent trials. Robust CSEs often appear in the prime-probe task, wherein an initial prime (usually a distractor) precedes a subsequent probe (usually a target). Recent findings indicate a CSE appears in mean probe reaction time (RT) and mean probe error rate (ER), however, even when participants respond to both the initial prime and the subsequent probe, such that there are no distractors (Grant & Weissman, 2019; Weissman, 2019; Weissman et al., 2017). Furthermore, a CSE appears in this “modified prime-probe task” even when subjects respond to the prime and probe in each trial using fingers on different hands (Weissman, Grant, and Jones, 2020). These findings indicate that “response-general” control processes (i.e., control processes that can modulate multiple responses) give rise to the CSE. However, several questions remain unanswered about the nature of response-general control processes.

title_r: Replication and Extension Sherf and Morrison (2020)
abstract_r: Sherf and Morrison (2020) describe that employees’ self-efficacy influences the perceived value of feedback and thus how much feedback they seek. Moreover, they argue that perspective taking plays a moderating role in the relation between self-efficacy and feedback-seeking. Sherf and Morrison (2020) measured employees' valuation of feedback and observed that it mediated the relation between self-efficacy and feedback-seeking, however, that was the only benefits and costs of feedback that the authors included in their model. A common assumption in the feedback-seeking literature is that when employees consider whether to ask for feedback they conduct a mental calculation of perceived benefits and costs of such feedback (Anseel et al., 2015; Ashford, 1986; Ashford & Cummings, 1983). Extending Sherf and Morrison (2020), in this study we will examine how self-efficacy and perspective taking influence various benefits and costs of asking for feedback. Specifically, we will look at: feedback expectancy value, self-presentation and ego costs, and self-presentation and ego benefits.

title_r: The Power-Sex Association and the Likelihood to Sexually Aggress: : A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Bargh, Raymond, Pryor, and Strack (1995)
abstract_r: The following study is a conceptual replication and extension of experiment two of Bargh, Raymond, Pryor, and Strack's (1995) paper. The experiment is translated into an online format, using Qualtrics. Updated measures have been used, in order to increase validity, and we are aiming to achieve a more representative sample. We are interested in seeing if the finding that men who are high in the likelihood to sexually aggress are more likely to find a woman more attractive if they have been primed with power, can be replicated. We also want to extend the research further to see if this relationship means that men would engage in sexually aggressive behaviour towards the female. In order to manipulate power, we will be using a word-fragment completion task using power-related words (as used in the original study). Participants will be exposed to a female confederate and asked to rate them on a series of attributes, including attractiveness. They will also be asked if they would like future contact with the confederate (through a skype call). We will be using a sexual aggression paradigm as a proxy for sexual aggression (described in the dependent variables section). To measure the likelihood to sexually aggress, we will be using the attraction to sexual aggression scale (Malamuth, 1989).
