title_r: Generating resistance to anti-vaccine conspiracy theories through inoculation messages: A conceptual replication study from Banas et al. (2023)
abstract_r: Inoculation is one of the communication strategies that can effectively generate resistance to conspiracy theories (O'Mahony et al., 2023; Banas & Miller, 2013; Banas et al., 2023). Many studies have been conducted to test the effectiveness of inoculation messages to confer resistance to various conspiracy theories, including 9/11 conspiracy theories (Banas & Miller, 2013) and anti-vaccine conspiracy theories (Banas et al., 2023). Inoculation messages involve two core components, (1) threat, messages that oppose arguments that the audience may encounter and (2) refutational preemption, the element within messages that will refute the weakened counterarguments by providing evidence and reasons to the person. Inoculation messages provide a weakened counterargument to influence persons with pre-bunking rather than debunking (contrasting counterarguments) to persuade others and change minds. The concept of inoculation messages is derived from inoculation theory that explains attitude and belief can be made resistant to persuasion (Compton & Pfau, 2005). This theory uses the medical analogy of vaccines to describe how weakened counter arguments within inoculation messages persuade people and change their attitudes. Aside from these, cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1975) is another foundation for inoculation messages. This theory describes that people are likely to change their attitudes when they are experiencing discomfort. Thus, inoculation messages through weakened counterarguments are the stimulus that may stimulate discomfort. This study will follow up the findings from Banas et al. (2023) where inoculation messages effectively generate resistance to anti-vaccine conspiracy theories. The study applied fact-based and logic-based inoculation messages describing the valid information about MMR vaccines and countering information from the movies, Vaxxed. Even though the message was specifically addressing MMR vaccines and anti-vaccine conspiracy theories, the logic-based inoculation was assumed to stimulate critical thinking that may be active to counter different conspiracy theories (e.g., Chemtrails, FEMA and Illuminati). However, designed inoculation messages failed to create cross protection towards other conspiracy theories. Thus, we assume that the inoculation message in this study is effective to confer resistance to conspiracy theories that are generated from misinformation, but not for conspiracy theories that are produced from conspiracy mentality. Conspiracy mentality or conspiracist ideation reflects a general worldview that some events occurred due to agreement between malicious and powerful parties (Bruder et al., 2013). Based on the study conducted by Imhoff et al. (2022), in terms of stability, conspiracy mentality is seen as a more stable trait compared to content-specific conspiracy theories, while content-specific conspiracy theories are seen as the symptom of conspiracy mentality. Therefore, we predict, participants with a high conspiracy mentality would still endorse anti-vaccine conspiracy theories, even after they are being exposed with the stimulus.

title_r: Motivational Anger Management Training: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication of Veenstra, Schneider, & Koole (2017) With a Virtual Reality-Based Serious Game
abstract_r: Recent findings indicate that letting people with chronic anger management problems make avoidance movements towards angry faces with a joystick lowers anger and aggression among this group (Veenstra, Schneider, & Koole, 2017). In the proposed study, we seek to conceptually replicate these findings. The proposed design is modelled after Study 2 of Veenstra, Schneider, and Koole (2017). Instead of joystick movements, however, we will manipulate whole body movements in a Virtual Reality (VR) environment among 78 undergraduate students. Participants with varying levels of trait anger will be randomly allocated to an experimental or control condition. In the experimental condition, participants will be instructed to lean backwards in response to avatars with angry facial expressions and to lean forward towards avatars with happy facial expressions. In the control condition, participants will receive the same instruction for happy-looking avatars, but not for angry-looking avatars, who will not appear in the VR environment. We predict that the experimental training will reduce anger and aggressive impulses among participants high (rather than low) in trait anger. The proposed study will provide a further test of embodied motivational models of anger management and fosters the development of VR-techniques that complements traditional cognitively based interventions.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: Direct replication of a research claim from Kang et al, 2009, in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Kang et al (2009) is: We selected the claim that for White faces, participants would see anger appear sooner and linger longer on an old compared to a young face, in line with research showing biases against White older adults (Statement 2), which reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Significant age by race interactions were observed: while participants perceived anger as lasting longer and appearing sooner on old compared to young White faces, this relationship was reversed for Black faces, with participants perceiving anger lasting longer and appearing sooner on young compared to old Black faces" (Statement 1). The claim is tested by using a paired-samples t-test, with target age as the predictor variable and time at which participants indicated that the first emotion had completely disappeared from the face as the outcome variable (Statement 3), from which it resulted that when observing White targets, participants judged anger as lasting longer on an old (M = 10.41 s, SD = 4.68s) compared to a young face (M = 8.86 s, SD = 4.35s), t(47) = -4.18, p = .001, d = -0.34. (Statement 4).

title_r: The effects of reading fiction on openmindedness: A replication and extension of Djikic et al. (2013)
abstract_r: This experiment aims to determine the way in which different kinds of reading open our minds and facilitate a more flexible thinking style. Djikic and colleagues (2013; Djikic, M., Oatley, K., & Moldoveanu, M. C. (2013). Opening the closed mind: The effect of exposure to literature on the need for closure. Creativity research journal, 25(2), 149-154.) observed that reading a fictional short story, when compared to reading a non-fictional essay, was associated with a significant decrease in self-reported need for cognitive closure. In the present experiment, we attempt to replicate and expand this finding. We will use the same reading stimuli used by Djikic and colleagues. In addition to the need for closure scale applied by these researchers, as dependent measures we will employ an openness scale, a cognitive complexity measure, an alternate uses task to index divergent thinking, and an imaginability task.

title_r: Callaway's (1960) Replication Study
abstract_r: This study implements a visual detection protocol where target presentation time is determined in real time, based on the phase within the alpha-frequency (5-15 Hz) estimated through EEG. This is a replication of a paper by E. Callaway published in Science in 1960. The main aim of the study is therefore to be able to send visual stimuli in a specific phase of the on-going alpha rhythm measured with EEG. The predicted result is that there is a correlation between the EEG phase at the moment of target onset and the reaction times to the stimuli at that phase.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Kool et al. (2010) at the University of Chicago
abstract_r: Sara Hockett, a fourth-year student at the University of Chicago, is replicating and extending the finding of Kool et al.'s (2010) experiment. This study found evidence supporting the law of least mental effort: that people will choose a less cognitively demanding course of action when given the opportunity. The current study will focus on the presence of this bias, which is hypothesized to exist even without direct awareness of a difference in cognitive demand. I hope to answer the question of whether anticipated cognitive demand is a significant element in decision making. The key test in the original study found that the option associated with higher cognitive was chosen more often than the option that was less cognitively demanding. We will also test if the high demand condition is higher than the low demand condition using the same analyses as in the original study. As an extension, I am also curious about whether the insufficient justification effect as it relates to cognitive dissonance could be induced regarding participants' appraisal of the tedious task. The insufficient justification effect argues that people will demonstrate positive attitude change towards an action they received insufficient justification for enacting. Such an attitude change reduces the cognitive dissonance arising between the effort of performing a tedious task and the lack of sufficient justification for doing so. We will test this effect with an experimental condition manipulating awareness of a gift-card prize for completion of the study. With this, we hope to answer the extent to which having extrinsic motivation for a dull task will reduce the cognitive dissonance of participants. Sara and her collaborators will be performing this study in efforts to attain her honors thesis in Psychology at the University of Chicago. A total of 130 participants will be collected so as to have 65 participants in each of the two conditions in the extension. The stopping point for data collection is the end of the University of Chicago's 2021 Spring Quarter.

title_r: Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication and Extension
abstract_r: The goal of this study is to replicate memory updating findings by Hupbach et al., 2007 (Experiment 1) and explore the impact of ad hoc category belongingness and stress on memory updating effects. Hupbach et al., 2007 had participants learn a list of objects at Session 1. Two days later, they learned a second list of objects at Session 2. Prior to learning the second list, some of the participants were reminded of the Session 1 learning experience (memory reactivation group) and some were not (no-reactivation group). When asked to recall the Session 1 list a couple days later at Session 3, participants in the memory reactivation group misattributed objects from Session 2 to Session 1 more often than participants in the no-reactivation group. We first aim to replicate this effect in an online version of the study (see “Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication” pre-registration). Next, we aim to explore the impact of using an ad hoc category of covid-related objects, instead of neutral unrelated objects as done in the original study, on memory updating effects. We will also include an additional control using an ad hoc category of beach-related objects, to account for ad hoc category belongingness in general. This pre-registration should be considered alongside the “Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication” pre-registration as the Neutral groups in this study comprise that replication. We have further described those groups and procedures in a separate pre-registration in order to make use of the Replication Recipe (Brandt et al., 2013) template.

title_r: Reductive Allure Effects for Psychology Phenomena – Impact of Worker Recruitment Site. A pre-registered replication of Hopkins, Weisberg, & Taylor (2016).
abstract_r: Previous research (Hopkins et al., 2016) suggests that the presentation of reductive information influences people’s ability to judge the quality of a scientific explanation. For instance, people who are presented with neuroscience jargon in an explanation of a psychological phenomenon judge those explanations more favorably than explanations without the jargon, even if that information is logically irrelevant. In a previously pre-registered (osf.io/hvm8q) attempt to replicate and extend Hopkins et al. (2016), we were unable to replicate this basic reductive explanation effect across three scientific disciplines that were included in the original study (Psychology, Neuroscience, Biology). That is, participants in our study did not rate reductive explanations significantly higher than horizontal explanations in any of these three scientific disciplines, even though we used the same testing materials and procedure as Hopkins et al. (2016). One possible explanation for our inability to replicate the reductive allure effect observed by Hopkins et al. (2016) is that we employed a different participant pool. Specifically, we recruited our participants from Prolific.co, whereas Hopkins et al. recruited participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Thus, in order to rule out the different participant pools as the reason for the discrepant results, we will conduct an abbreviated replication of Hopkins et al. (2016) using only their original descriptions of psychological phenomena (the scientific discipline that showed the largest reductive explanation effect) with a participant pool selected from Amazon Mechanical Turk.

title_r: Are visuospatial and empathic perspective-taking associated on a dispositional level? A preregistered replication of Erle & Topolinski (2015)
abstract_r: Erle and Topolinski (2015, https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2015.33.3.187) reported a negative correlation between response time (RT) for a visuospatial perspective-taking (VPT) task and empathic perspective-taking skill, as measured by the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), in their Study 4. However, Migita and Inoue (2023, https://doi.org/10.2132/personality.31.3.8) failed to replicate this finding using an online experiment with Japanese participants. The present study aims to examine whether the results of Study 4 from Erle and Topolinski (2015) can be replicated in the Japanese population by revising the experimental procedure used by Migita and Inoue (2023). Specifically, the present study will (1) present stimulus images of an East Asian man and woman to Japanese participants (Migita and Inoue used images of a German man and woman, which were the same stimuli as those used by Erle and Topolinski, 2015), (2) control the physical sizes of the presented stimuli using a calibration procedure prior to the experimental task, and (3) measure participants’ choice reaction time to control for interpersonal variability of RT unrelated to VPT.

abstract_r: The original study investigated skilled and adaptive strategy selection in risky decision making. We wish to replicate the effect shown by Traczyk et al. (2018), where people with higher objective statistical numeracy (measured by Berlin Numeracy Test, BNT, Cokely et al., 2012), in comparison to people with lower numeracy, adaptively select choice strategy depending on the task structure or the characteristics of the environment. Put differently, highly numerate people do not use more effortful strategies unless it is strictly required; in trivial choice problems, they employ fast and frugal heuristic processing, but in meaningful problems, they engage more elaborate and effortful information processing. We propose that people with high objective statistical numeracy are able to learn the importance of the decision problems. If it is meaningful, they are likely to deliberate longer to make a superior decision, making choices consistent with predictions of more effortful and reward maximizing choice strategies predicted by Cumulative Prospect Theory/Expected Value (CPT/EV) theory, but if the decision problems are trivial and lead to comparable payoffs, they make faster but normatively suboptimal choices consistent with predictions of fast and frugal priority heuristic (PH). Numerate decision makers don’t use more eﬀortful strategies unless it pays: A process tracing investigation of skilled and adaptive strategy selection in risky decision making. title_r: Study 4 - Conceptual replication of Tobia (2016)
abstract_r: Past research by Kevin Tobia (2016) suggests that dramatic changes in a person's character are seen as more detrimental to this person's personal identity when changes are negative (=deteroriation) rather than positive (=improvement). Moreover, Tobia (2016) observed that these identity judgments were reflected in people's right to access and erase sensible data about their old self. However, one worry is that the measure of personal identity used in these studies might have been inadequate to the extent that they failed to distinguish between numeric and qualitative identity. To test for this possibility, our goal in this study is to reproduce Kevin Tobia's study while comparing the results for three different measures of personal identity (traditional, new and alternate).

title_r: Does Tolerance Allow Bonobos to Outperform Chimpanzees on a Cooperative Task? A conceptual replication of Hare et al., 2007
abstract_r: By replicating a cornerstone experimental study on tolerance and cooperation in bonobos and chimpanzees (Hare et al., 2007 Cur. Biol. 17, 619–623), we aim to understand whether current discrepant findings may result from noise, methodological differences, or behavioural variability. We tested bonobos and chimpanzees housed at the same facility in a co-feeding and cooperation task. Food was placed on dishes located on both ends or in the middle of a platform. In the co-feeding task, the tray was simply made available to the ape duos, whereas in the cooperation task the apes had to simultaneously pull at both ends of a rope attached to the platform to retrieve the food.

title_r: Combining manipulations of working memory and individual-difference approaches to explore the dependence of distractor devaluation on working memory resources: A conceptual replication and extension of Goolsby et al. (2009)
abstract_r: Stimuli appearing as distractors in visual-search tasks subsequently receive more negative affective ratings than novel stimuli or the targets of attention. By demonstrating that this ‘distractor-devaluation effect’ is eliminated with a concurrent visual working-memory load, Goolsby et al. (2009) provided evidence that visual working memory resources may be important for encoding associative links between the perceptual details of a distractor and the cognitive-affective processes that lead it to receive negative evaluations. The current project provides a conceptual replication and extension of Goolsby et al. by using a similar within-participant experimental manipulation of level of concurrent working-memory load during the measurement of distractor devaluation, while also using an individual-difference approach to provide a converging test of the hypothesis that distractor devaluation requires working-memory resources. Furthermore, by using a battery of different working-memory capacity measurement tasks to assess individual differences in various aspects of visual storage capacity and attention-related working-memory abilities, the present work seeks to test whether the role of visual working memory in mediating distractor devaluation primarily concerns the mere maintenance of visual information, or the active manipulation of information during working-memory maintenance. Our project also builds on Goolsby et al.by changing the type of stimuli and increasing their number in the task used to measure distractor devaluation. Support for the hypothesis that distractor devaluation requires visual working memory resources would be evident in 1) a replication of the finding that distractor devaluation is eliminated with a concurrent visual working memory load but occurs without a load, and 2) the finding that the magnitude of distractor devaluation is reduced in participants with relatively low visual-working memory capacities when compared to that obtained in individuals with relatively high visual-working memory capacities. If the role of visual working memory in mediating distractor devaluation concerns the maintenance of visual information, then individual differences in the magnitude of distractor devaluation should be predicted by differences in the performance of those individuals in any working-memory task that is sensitive to the number of visual representations that can be simultaneously maintained in working memory. If the role of visual working memory in mediating distractor devaluation concerns the active manipulation of information during working-memory maintenance, then individual differences in the magnitude of distractor devaluation should be predicted by performance differences only in the working-memory tasks that require attentional selection during memory maintenance. Given our lab’s interest in boredom as a manifestation of negative affect linked to difficulties with attentional engagement, the present project also includes an exploratory assessment of the link between individual differences in the tendency to experience boredom (i.e., trait boredom proneness) and individual differences in the magnitude of distractor devaluation.

title_r: The Effect of Guilt and Shame on Construal Level : A Preregistered Replication Study of Han et al. (2014)
abstract_r: The purpose of this study is to replicate the effect of guilt and shame on construal level found by Han et al. (2014). Using autobiographical recall, we will induce either guilt or shame. That is, participants will have 10 minutes to recall an event that made them feel either guilt or shame and describe it as precisely as possible (conditions surrounding this event, feelings and thoughts associated). Participants in the control condition will have 10 minutes to describe a typical day in their life. Then, we will measure participants' construal level using the Behavior Identification Form (BIF, Wegner & Vallacher, 1989). We will use a translated and validated French version of this questionnaire (Belayachi & Van der Linden, unpublished), which contains 23 items. Specifically, we will ask participants to read action verbs (e.g., taking a test) and to choose which option, among two (e.g., answering questions [low-level construal] VS showing one’s knowledge [high-level construal]), describes better the way they represent the target action. After this measure, participants will rate the extent to which they feel guilt and shame (i.e., as a manipulation check). We will then measure psychological distance following Fiedler et al. (2012), by showing participants an action verb and ask them to imagine a situation in which they would engage themselves in a situation prompted by this action verb, to briefly describe the situation, and to judge the distance of the imagined situation concerning the social, temporal, spatial and probability distance dimensions. The psychological distance isn’t part of the original study, but we added it at the end in a more exploratory perspective in order to investigate the effect of these emotions on perceived psychological distance. Hence, we expect that (H1) participants in the guilt condition will have a lower construal level score than participants in the shame condition, with the control condition falling in between. This hypothesis is derived from Han et al. (2014) and is our replication and main hypothesis. We also expect that (H2) participants in the guilt condition will have a lower psychological distance score than participants in the shame condition, with the control condition falling in between. This constitutes our secondary hypothesis and we derive it from the Construal level theory (Trope et al, 2007; Trope et Liberman, 2010; Liberman, 2007).

title_r: How strong is the rhythm of perception? A registered replication of Hickok, Farahbod, and Saberi (2015)
abstract_r: Our ability to predict upcoming events is a fundamental component of human cognition. One way in which we do so is to exploit temporal regularities in sensory signals: the ticking of a clock, falling of footsteps, and the motion of waves each provide a structure that may facilitate anticipation. But how strong is the effect of rhythmic anticipation on perception? And to what degree do people vary in their ability to capitalize on these regularities? Hickok, Farahbod, and Saberi (2015) introduced a behavioral paradigm to assess how a rhythmic auditory stimulus affects perception of subsequent targets. They tested five listeners, and found that perception – that is, target detection accuracy – fluctuated rhythmically just like the sound rhythm. Here we aim to replicate the original finding, to assess how likely the finding is to be observed for any individual, and to quantify effect size in a relatively large sample of listeners. We introduce a model-based approach for analyzing the data that allows separate estimates of amplitude and phase information in target detection responses, and quantifies effect size for individual listeners.

title_r: Conceptual replication of Dignath et al., 2022, experiment 3 - particular focus on emotional Stroop task (E.g., Soutscheck and Schubert, 2013) 'Do self-related primes influence the processing of conflicts in the emotional domain?'
abstract_r: Previous research has shown (e.g., Dignath et al., 2022) that Congruency Effects (CE) in a gender Stroop task are significantly reduced when self-related primes are used compared neutral primes in a control condition. The significant interaction of the factors ‘congruency’ and ‘prime’, indicated reduced CEs in experimental blocks with self-referential information compared to control blocks. Here, we ask whether this phenomenon can be replicated also in the emotional domain. We will closely replicate experiment 3 of Dignath et al. (2022), but instead of a gender task, emotional Stroop task will be employed (modelled after Soutscheck & Schubert, 2013), in which participants must classify facial expressions as positive or negative, while ignoring clearly positive or negative valenced words. In line with the study of Dignath et al. (2022), the main question of this experiment is how self-referential primes modulate CEs. Going beyond previous research, we ask whether similar effects can be generalized to the emotional domain. We consider two possible accounts. The attentional bias account assumes that CEs should be increased in the self-referential condition, because self-referential primes draw attention towards the task-irrelevant dimension and hence should enhance CEs. Specifically, for emotional stimuli, it has been suggested that attention is not only quicker engaged by emotional stimuli, but also impairs attentional disengagement. In contrast, the priming of control account holds that CEs in the self-referential condition should be reduced, because self-relevance boosts cognitive control over task-irrelevant response tendencies. Indeed, it has been suggested that the inextricable link between control and self-referential information is particularly strong for emotional material.

title_r: Migration, Diversity, and Economic Growth. A Replication Study of Bove and Elia (World Development, 2017)

(2016), only migration maintains a positive impact on growth while diversity, as captured by fractionalization, turns out to be weakly and positively associated with growth, but limitedly to the 1980-2010 time span.Polarization, on the other hand, does not seem to exert any effect on growth.The question as to whether diversity is more or less beneficial in terms of economic growth remains therefore an intriguing one, and calls for more theoretical and empirical analyses, possibly based on less (geographically) aggregated data.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

title_r: Replicating and Extending Experiment 1 from Garcea and Mahon (2012) using only picture stimuli
abstract_r: In daily life, when we need to have a drink, we try to find a cup. Would we find it faster according to the object's function or based on the manipulation of the object? Garcea and Mahon (2012) used a modified neuropsychological test that used the response time (RT) and accuracy as the dependent measures. Three objects were presented in a triangular arrangement at the same time in one trial. The top object was the target. One of the two lower objects had a similar function to the target object, and the other had a similar manipulation to the target object. The participants had to judge which object of a triad had a similar function to the target object or which object had a similar manipulation to the target. Results showed that manipulation judgments were slower than function judgments, regardless of whether the objects were shown as words or as pictures. This finding suggests that it is unnecessary to first retrieve knowledge of object manipulation before one can retrieve knowledge of object function (Garcea & Mahon, 2012). The results of Garcea and Mahon contrast with the outcomes of another study (Ruotolo & Kalénine, 2020). Ruotolo and Kalénine (2020) used the Visual-World-Paradigm to present four objects to the participants at the same time. One of the four objects was the target. The rest of the objects were distractors that could have a similar function as the target, or a similar manipulation, or be completely unrelated to the target. They found that distractors with similar functions or manipulations attracted more attention from participants than unrelated distractors. Moreover, the results showed that eye fixations to objects with a similar manipulation occurred faster relative to the objects with a similar function. This is in contrast with Garcea and Mahon’s study, as it suggests that similarity in manipulation leads to quicker attentional orienting than similarity in function. In the current experiment, we will replicate Experiment 1 of Garcea and Mahon (2012), using only the condition with object pictures. Aside from testing the replicability of Garcea and Mahon’s finding of faster reaction times for function than for manipulation similarity, we will also examine whether differences in real-world size might have contributed to this difference in reaction time. Specifically, we reasoned that one explanation for the finding of slower manipulation judgments than function judgments in Garcea and Mahon (2012) could be that if the target object and two lower objects in the stimulus displayed differed in their real-world size in some trials, this might have caused participants to be slower on these trials as they would need to imagine the manipulation of two objects (the target and the non-target) of different sizes in the real world to decide which one matches the target. Arguably, this would slow participants down (because it takes more time to imagine two manipulations for objects that differ in real-world size than to imagine the manipulation for two objects with similar real-world size), and it, therefore, could explain why this study found slower RTs for manipulation judgments. In replicating the experiment, we are able to make use of the exact same stimuli as Garcea and Mahon (2012), as they kindly made these available to us. According to the classification from Fisher and Sperandio (2018), 10 of the 35 objects used by Garcea and Mahon can be classified as ”big objects” and the rest of the objects can be classified as “small objects”. Among the 24 triads used for function judgments and manipulation judgments, 8 triads were comprised of objects of different sizes. Hence, we speculate that the object size may be an important factor in the previous experiment and it may affect the results. Accordingly, we hypothesize that manipulation judgments are only slower than function judgments when objects in the triad differ in real-world size.

title_r: Brough_JournConsRes_2016_9ey - Brough - Direct Replication - z161
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Brough et al 2016 is the Study 2 claim that participants who read about a character (either male or female) doing a green behavior (using a reusable shopping bag) give higher ratings of stereotypically female traits to that character. This claim is based on the following sentence from the paper’s abstract: “[C]onsumers who engage in green behaviors are stereotyped by others as more feminine”. The claim is tested using an F test on an index for femininity constructed from three rating items, with target’s behavior (green or non green) and gender (male or female) as independent variables. This analysis yielded that the femininity index differed significantly based on the target’s environmental behavior; F(1, 190) = 44.00, p < .001, partial eta squared = .19, such that the green target (M = 2.64, SD = .90, N = 94) was perceived as more feminine than the non green target (M = 1.82, SD = .86, N = 100).

title_r: First language effects on incidental vocabulary learning through bimodal input: A multisite, preregistered, and close replication of Malone (2018)
abstract_r: This multi-site preregistered study aims to replicate and extend Malone (2018), who investigated how the effects of providing aural enhancement (i.e., reading-while-listening) on incidental vocabulary learning and the moderating role of the number of exposure to target words (two vs. four times) as well as learner’s working memory capacity. The current study is a close replication of Malone (2018) (see e.g., Porte & McManus, 2019 for a typology of replication studies), meaning that we intend to only manipulate one variable: participants’ L1 backgrounds by specifically recruiting learners whose first language is Chinese, Dutch, or German. At the same time, we will follow the study protocol of the initial study as closely as possible. Our overall hypothesis is that L1 background can have an effect on reading-while-listening vocabulary learning under incidental contexts. More specifically, we hypothesize that aural enhancement will be more beneficial for learners whose first language is opaque in terms of grapheme-phoneme correspondence (e.g., Chinese) than those whose native language is transparent (e.g., Germanic languages). Our hypothesis was guided by theory that suggests the intimate relationship between L1 phoneme-grapheme mapping and L2 phonological decoding efficiency, which in turn influences the way learners read in the L2 (e.g., Wang et al., 2003) and learn L2 words (e.g., Hamada & Koda, 2008). We will recruit participants on multiple sites, including Innsbruck (Austria), Leuven (Belgium), Beijing (China), and Hong Kong (China). Following the initial study, we will examine how (a) the aural enhancement (reading-while-listening vs. reading only), (b) the number of target words (two vs. four times), and (c) working memory capacity influence learning of vocabulary under incidental conditions, in addition to our new variable, (d) participants’ L1 backgrounds (Chinese vs. Germanic). We have been invited to contribute to a special issue of Studies in Second Language Acquisition guest edited by Kevin McManus under a theme of replication research in SLA.

title_r: Do LLMs Exhibit Human-Like Bayesian Judgment and Moral Inconsistency? A Replication Study of Cao et al. (2019)
abstract_r: This study replicates Cao et al. (2019) People Make the Same Bayesian Judgment They Criticize in Others using Large Language Models (LLMs) rather than human participants. Cao et al. (2019) found that humans exhibit an inconsistency in their responses - they make statistically accurate Bayesian judgments about profession likelihood based on gender, while simultaneously condemning others who make identical judgments. We examine whether contemporary LLMs (Claude Sonnet 3.7 and GPT-4o) display similar patterns of inconsistency. By comparing LLMs with different training methods and company missions, we attempt to identify whether algorithmic systems trained on human data inherit our inconsistencies or behave as more consistently Bayesian agents. This research helps our understanding of alignment in LLM systems, particularly regarding how different approaches to LLM development affect statistical reasoning versus encoded social norms.

title_r: Effects of the Generic Masculine and its Alternatives in Germanophone countries. A Multi-lab Replication and Extension of Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun, 2001
abstract_r: In languages such as German, French, or Hindi, plural forms of job occupations and societal roles are often in a generic-masculine form instead of a gender-neutral form. Although meant as “generic”, this generic-masculine form excludes women from everyday language and might even entail the cognitive effect that listeners and readers will less likely think of women. Several studies have demonstrated this and related cognitive effects in the past. Due to the societal relevance of gender-neutral language, we propose a direct replication and extension of a classic study by Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun (2001, Experiment 2) in a multi-lab setting. We already present preliminary evidence showing that people indeed come up with more female exemplars when they are asked to name celebrities from several domains, such as politics and sports in gender-neutral forms compared to the generic-masculine form. The proposed multi-lab study will be conducted among 12 labs, collecting data from more than N = 2,000 participants.

title_r: Not toeing the number line for simple arithmetic: Two large-n conceptual replications of Mathieu et al. (Cognition, 2016, Experiment 1)
abstract_r: We conducted two conceptual replications of Experiment 1 in Mathieu, Gourjon, Couderc, Thevenot, and Prado (2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2015.10.002). They tested a sample of 34 French adults on mixed-operation blocks of single-digit addition (4 + 3) and subtraction (4 – 3) with the three problem elements (O1, +/-, O2) presented sequentially. Addition was 34 ms faster if O2 appeared 300 ms after the operation sign and displaced 5° to the right of central fixation, whereas subtraction was 19 ms faster when O2 was displaced to the left. Replication Experiment 1 (n = 74 recruited at the University of Saskatchewan) used the same non-zero addition and subtraction problems and trial event sequence as Mathieu et al., but participants completed blocks of pure addition and pure subtraction followed by the mixed-operation condition used by Mathieu et al. Addition RT showed a 32 ms advantage with O2 shifted rightward relative to leftward but only in mixed-operation blocks. There was no effect of O2 position on subtraction RT. Experiment 2 (n = 74) was the same except mixed-operation blocks occurred before the pure-operation blocks. There was an overall 13 ms advantage with O2 shifted right relative to leftward but no interaction with operation or with mixture (i.e., pure vs mixed operations). Nonetheless, the rightward RT advantage was statistically significant for both addition and subtraction only in mixed-operation blocks. Taken together with the robust effects of mixture in Experiment 1, the results suggest that O2 position effects in this paradigm might reflect task specific demands associated with mixed operations.

title_r: How strong is the rhythm of perception? A registered replication of Hickok et al. (2015)
abstract_r: Our ability to predict upcoming events is a fundamental component of human cognition. One way in which we do so is by exploiting temporal regularities in sensory signals: the ticking of a clock, falling of footsteps and the motion of waves each provide a structure that may facilitate anticipation. But how strong is the effect of rhythmic anticipation on perception? And to what degree do people vary in their ability to capitalize on these regularities? In 2015, Hickok et al. introduced a behavioural paradigm to assess how a rhythmic auditory stimulus affects perception of subsequent targets (Hickok G, Farahbod H, Saberi K. 2015 The rhythm of perception: entrainment to acoustic rhythms induces subsequent perceptual oscillation. Psychol. Sci. 26, 1006–1013. (doi:10.1177/0956797615576533)). They tested five listeners and found that perception (target detection accuracy) fluctuated rhythmically just like the sound rhythm. Here, we replicate the original finding, assess how likely the finding is to be observed for any individual, and quantify effect size in a large sample of adult listeners (n = 149). We introduce a model-based analysis approach that allows separate estimates of amplitude and phase information in target detection responses, and quantifies effect size for individual listeners. Together our results strongly support the presence of oscillatory influences on target detection accuracy, as well as substantial variability in the magnitude of this effect across listeners.

title_r: Market Access and Quality Upgrading: Evidence from Four Field Experiments. A Replication Study of Bold et al. (American Economic Review, 2022)
abstract_r: Bold et al. (2022) investigate the effect of providing access to a larger, centralized market where quality is rewarded with a premium on farm productivity and framing incomes from smallholder maize farmers in western Uganda, using a series of randomized experiments and a difference-in-differences approach. We successfully reproduce the results of this study using the publicly provided replication packet. Then test the robustness of these results by re-defining treatment and outcome variables, testing for model misspecification and the leverage of outliers, and testing for non-random selection in the Fisher-permutation process. Our results show that the findings in Bold et al. (2022) are robust to a variety of decisions in the research process. This evokes confidence in the internal validity of the findings.

title_r: Migration, Diversity, and Economic Growth. A Replication Study of Bove and Elia (World Development, 2017)
abstract_r: A recent and well known paper, Bove and Elia (2017), argues that migrants' diversity, as captured by the indexes of both fractionalization and polarization, exerts a positive effect on GDP growth. In fact, by using the same dataset and methodology, we show that the impact of diversity cannot be distinguished from that of migration itself due to the very high correlation among the corresponding variables. Also, if one disentangles migration from diversity, following Alesina et al. (2016), only migration maintains a positive impact on growth while diversity, as captured by fractionalization, turns out to be weakly and positively associated with growth, but limitedly to the 1980-2010 time span. Polarization, on the other hand, does not seem to exert any effect on growth. The question as to whether diversity is more or less beneficial in terms of economic growth remains therefore an intriguing one, and calls for more theoretical and empirical analyses, possibly based on less (geographically) aggregated data.

title_r: Meta-analysis and publication bias: How well does the FAT-PET-PEESE procedure work? A replication study of Alinaghi & Reed (Research Synthesis Methods, 2018)
abstract_r: This R-code produces the results of the replication study. Abstract of the paper: A meta-analysis is a tool for aggregating estimates of a similar “effect” across many studies. Publication bias is the phenomenon where literature is sample selected in favor of studies having statistically significant results and/or having estimates that satisfy pre-conceived expectations. A popular procedure used for conducting meta-analyses in the presence of publication bias is the FAT-PET-PEESE (FPP) procedure. In a recent paper published in \emph{Research Synthesis Methods}, Alinaghi and Reed (2018), utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, report that the FPP procedure does not work well when used in “realistic” data environments where true effects differ both across and within studies. AR’s findings are important because the FPP approach is dominant in the economics meta-analysis literature. I replicate their results and discover two mistakes, which I subsequently correct. The first mistake is found in a descriptive statistics table, misrepresenting the overview of simulated dataset. The second is associated with the fixed effect estimation, generating erroneous estimated effects and Type I error. Further, I extend their analysis by making their simulation environment even more realistic. Despite producing somewhat different results, my replications generally confirm AR’s conclusions about the unreliability of the FPP procedure in realistic data environments.

title_r: Lowe_JournMarketRes_2017_VGAe - Hannon - Direct Replication
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Lowe and Haws (2017) is that lower (higher) auditory pitch used in marketing communications cues inferences of larger (smaller) physical size in the associated product. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Through six studies, the authors find that when associated with a product, lower pitch in voice or music leads consumers to infer a larger product size." The claim is tested by assigning participants to hear an advertisement for a new sandwich at a fictitious sandwich chain in one of two auditory conditions (high-voice condition and low-voice condition). The dependent variable was participant ratings of their perception of the size of the advertised sandwich, using a seven-point scale anchored on “much smaller than average” and “much larger than average.” Consistent with the prediction, participants who heard the advertisement featuring the lower voice believed the advertised sandwich was significantly larger than those who heard the higher-pitched version (Mlow = 4.87 (SD = 1.20) vs. Mhigh = 4.29 (SD = 1.01); F(1, 93) = 6.38, p < .05).

title_r: A Conceptual Replication of Mussweiler and Strack (2000) Study 1
abstract_r: This study is a conceptual replication of Study 1 by Mussweiler and Strack (2000), which tested the Selective Accessibility Model (SAM) of the anchoring effect. SAM explains anchoring as the selective activation of anchor-consistent knowledge through hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. In their study, participants completed a standard anchoring task (estimating Germany’s mean annual temperature, with anchors set at either 5 or 20 degrees) followed by a Lexical Decision Task (LDT). The results supported SAM, showing faster responses to winter words in the LDT under the low-anchor condition. Our study is a conceptual replication of their study, conducted online to assess the reproducibility of the effect.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Mussweiler and Strack (2000, Study 2) Using Temperature Anchoring and a Season-Related LDT (2)
abstract_r: This study conceptually replicates Study 2 by Mussweiler and Strack (2000), which tested the Selective Accessibility Model (SAM) of the anchoring effect. According to SAM, anchoring occurs through the selective activation of anchor-consistent knowledge, driven by hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. In the original study, participants first completed a standard comparative anchoring task (judging whether the average price of a new car was higher or lower than U.S. $11,000 or $22,000), followed by a Lexical Decision Task (LDT). After the LDT, they estimated the average price of a new car in an absolute judgment task. The results supported SAM, demonstrating a significant interaction between anchor condition and word type in the LDT. In the present study, we conducted a conceptual replication of this design, using an anchoring task involving temperature estimates and an LDT employing season-related words (summer- and winter-related words). Data collection was completed on June 10, 2025 (Japan Standard Time). As of this preregistration, the data have not yet been accessed or analyzed. This preregistration specifies the planned analysis procedures. The majority of the experimental procedures and hypotheses follow Mussweiler and Strack (2000) and our previous study (https://osf.io/hcbxu, https://osf.io/wgm94, https://osf.io/57cty).

title_r: Independent Direct Replication of Vess (2012, PS, Study 1)
abstract_r: The main goal of the current project is to execute an independent (direct) replication of Vess’ (2012, PS) main finding from his Study 1. Consistent with an embodiment account, he found that more anxiously attached individuals reported more desire for warm food and drinks, but only when such individuals had recalled a past romantic breakup (vs. recalling an ordinary event). We will execute a high-powered (estimated power of .95) independent replication using exactly the same measures, manipulations, instructions (exact instructions and manipulation acquired from Vess), and sampling approach (online sample using Amazon’s Mechanical Turk website). The primary goal is to determine whether Vess’ finding generalizes to a new sample of individuals, hence contributing to the question of whether Vess' original finding reflects reproducible knowledge.

title_r: "Explaining How Long CO2 Stays in the Atmosphere: Does It Change Attitudes Toward Climate Change?" - a replication study (Joslyn & Demnitz, 2021)
abstract_r: Aus wissenschaftlicher Perspektive ist ein kritischer Punkt der globalen Erwärmung erreicht (Ripple et al., 2017). Trotzdem scheint die Wahrnehmung von Risiken bezüglich des Klimawandels erheblich zwischen Ländern (Eurobarometer, 2014) und Individuen (Botzen et al., 2016) zu variieren. Häufig wird der Klimawandel als ein zeitlich und räumlich entferntes Problem wahrgenommen (Lorenzoni & Hulme, 2009). Insbesondere Menschen mit einer konservativen politischen Ideologie scheinen dem Klimawandel dabei kritisch gegenüberzustehen (Funk & Rainie, 2015). Um zu überprüfen, wie sich diese Einstellungen zum Klimawandel verändern lassen, untersuchten Joslyn und Demnitz (2021) anhand einer repräsentativen nationalen Stichprobe aus den USA die Auswirkungen von zwei einfachen Strategien der Klimakommunikation auf das Verständnis und die Reaktion auf den Klimawandel bei verschiedenen politischen Ideologien. Dabei kamen sie zu dem Ergebnis, dass psychologisch gezielte Klimakommunikation die Einstellung zur globalen Erwärmung unabhängig von politischer Ideologie verändern kann. Mit dem Ziel, das derzeitige Wissen über den Einfluss psychologisch gezielter Klimakommunikation auf die Einstellungen zum Klimawandel in verschiedenen Ländern und Kulturen zu erweitern, wird die Studie von Joslyn und Demnitz (2021) in der vorliegenden Studie im Kontext der deutschen Bevölkerung repliziert. Dabei wollen wir unter anderem dem in der Psychologie weit verbreiteten Phänomen Rechnung tragen, dass Replikationen viel zu selten durchgeführt und veröffentlicht werden (Neuliep & Crandall, 1993) und zum Aufbau einer kumulativen Wissensbasis beitragen (Brandt et al., 2014; Dekkers et al., 2010).

title_r: A replication and extension of Scott and Landy (2023): moral character beliefs about medical treatment options
abstract_r: Treatment adherence is a known problem in healthcare. For example, low medication use and adherence are noticed in patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disorder (COPD), even with a severe diagnosis (Ingebrigtsen et al., 2014). Likewise, psychiatric medication has stigma attached to it which increases the reluctance of patients to take medication. Research has shown that adolescents on psychiatric medication limited social interactions due to the shame which accompanies stigma (Kranke et al., 2010). One area to explain low treatment adherence are beliefs associated with specific treatments: for example, research has shown that the use of medication instead of behavioural or lifestyle changes is perceived to be a signal of lower willpower (Scott & Landy, 2023), while working hard and applying effort (i.e, willpower) is a socially acceptable positive moral characteristic (Amos et al., 2017). Scott and Landy's (2023) work on moral judgements about medical treatment options therefore laid the groundwork for understanding the influence of moral virtues on medical decision-making. The study revealed a bias, with a preference for behavioural or lifestyle changes over pharmaceutical interventions as it is perceived to be reflective of a stronger moral character. The current study is a partial replication and an extension of Scott and Landy's (2023) work on moral judgements about medical treatment options. The present study aims to explore this theme in the contexts of physical health (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disorder; COPD), mental health (Depression) and neurodivergent conditions (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder). In their original study, Scott and Landy include COPD and depression, but did not compare these directly; that is, they did not examine if the effect of treatment type on moral judgements differed by type of conditions, which we expect to find given the known stigma around mental health and neurodivergence (Kranke et al., 2010). In summary, there is one main research question for this study. RQ: Does the effect of treatment type on moral judgements vary by type of conditions? References: Amos, C., Zhang, L., & Read, D. (2017). Hardworking as a heuristic for moral character: Why we attribute moral values to those who work hard and its implications. Journal of Business Ethics, 158(4), 1047–1062. Ingebrigtsen, T. title_r: “Your Brain On Video Games”: A re-analysis, replication and extension of Martinez et al. (2023)
abstract_r: This research is being carried out in the context of a second year Master’s dissertation. The field of research on the psychology of video games is about as divided as it is recent (Chaput, 2023). Studies and meta-analyses alike cannot seem to reach a consensus about the effects of this relatively new media on affects, socialisation, or cognitive performance. Among several concerns, the field suffers from a lack of unity in terminology, research methods, and analytical models (Elson & Ferguson, 2014). The issue is further illustrated in psychological research at large, as evidenced by the current replicability crisis (Balafoutas et al., 2025; Rouphael, 2022). To overcome the matter, several good practices are recommended by experts in the field, such as replication and accountability. The present study therefore aims to replicate a recent study on the psychology of video game play, investigating the links between playing practice and cognitive performance (Martinez et al., 2023). The proposed replication follows a first phase of thorough re-analysis of the original clean dataset, which was made available in open access by the authors. In this second phase, new data will be collected to re-assess the original findings, using updated analytical models. Furthermore, we will extend the original protocol by investigating two additional relevant variables, which were not previously taken into account: participants’ starting age of video game practice (Hambrick et al., 2014) and overall level of cognitive performance (Matton et al., 2022; Wolfram, 2023). Throughout the entire project, we are involving the authors of the original study (Dr Léa Martinez, Dr Manuel Gimenes and Dr Eric Lamber), who kindly volunteered their materials for the purposes of this replication. In addition to this pre-registration, we will be sharing the full anonymised dataset in open access after data collection is completed. With this project, we aim to further our understanding of the links between video game practice and cognition, as well as to contribute to better practices in video game research. title_r: Petersen_Cognition_2017_yJwG - Snyder - Direct Replication - 9ky
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Petersen et al. (2017) is from Experiment 1, in which participants were to report the identity of a post-masked letter that was presented for varying exposure durations immediately after an auditory cue or no cue. Equations based on a theory of visual attention were fit to the data for each participant (see equations p. 74), separately for cue and no-cue trials, with the result that the parameter for processing speed (v) was faster following an auditory cue, compared to no-cue trials. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “[P]hasic auditory alertness affects visual perception by increasing the visual processing speed and lowering the threshold of conscious perception (Experiment 1).” Using the equations shown on page 74, for each condition (no cue, 85 dB cue), v and t0 parameters were estimated separately for each subject by a maximum-likelihood estimation using the Nelder-Mead simplex optimization algorithm. To improve the estimation of parameters, a high-threshold guessing model was introduced, which assumes that with a certain probability, subjects guess randomly among the 20 letters if they fail to encode the presented letter into visual short term memory. Paired t tests were used to compare these parameter values between conditions. This analysis yielded that there was faster processing speed v, t(27) = 4.71, p < 0.001, dz = 0.89, and a lower perceptual threshold t0, t(27) = 3.52, p = 0.002, dz = 0.67, when an 85 dB SPL cue is presented prior to the letter, compared to when no cue was present.

title_r: Individual differences in receptivity to scientific bullshit: a pre-registered replication study of Evans et al. (2020).
abstract_r: Research on the processes underlying bullshit receptivity is underway to understand why people are influenced by misinformation and how it operates. Evans et al. (2020) extended existing research by introducing a new measure of scientific bullshit receptivity, building on previous research on pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity (Pennycook et al., 2015). They also examined how the two types of bullshit receptivity, pseudo-profound and scientific, are related to factors such as belief in science, political conservatism, and individual differences in need for cognition. As a result, strong positive correlations emerged between the two types of bullshit receptivity, and both were positively correlated with belief in science, political conservatism, and faith in intuition. These results remained robust when controlling for acquiescence bias. Furthermore, scientific bullshit sensitivity was positively correlated with belief in science and negatively correlated with political conservatism and faith in intuition. To test the cultural generalizability of these results, the present study conducts a pre-registered replication of Study 2 by Evans et al. (2020) with Japanese participants.

title_r: Reductive Allure Effects for Psychology Phenomena – Impact of Worker Recruitment Screening. A Pre-Registered Replication of Hopkins, Weisberg, & Taylor (2016).
abstract_r: Previous research (Hopkins et al., 2016) suggests that the presentation of reductive information influences people’s ability to judge the quality of a scientific explanation. For instance, people who are presented with neuroscience jargon in an explanation of a psychological phenomenon judge those explanations more favorably than explanations without the jargon, even if that information is logically irrelevant. In a previously pre-registered (osf.io/hvm8q) attempt to replicate and extend Hopkins et al. (2016), we were unable to replicate this basic reductive explanation effect across three scientific disciplines that were included in the original study (Psychology, Neuroscience, Biology). That is, participants in our study did not rate reductive explanations significantly higher than horizontal explanations in any of these three scientific disciplines, even though we used the same testing materials and procedure as Hopkins et al. (2016). One possible explanation for our inability to replicate the reductive allure effect observed by Hopkins et al. (2016) is that we employed a different participant pool. Specifically, we recruited our participants from Prolific.co, whereas Hopkins et al. recruited participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Thus, in order to rule out the different participant pools as the reason for the discrepant results, we conducted a second pre-registered experiment (osf.io/8af7k) to examine the effects of worker platform. In that second experiment, we conducted an abbreviated replication of Hopkins et al. (2016) using only their original descriptions of psychological phenomena (the scientific discipline that showed the largest reductive explanation effect) with a participant pool selected from Amazon Mechanical Turk. In this second experiment, we were again unable to replicate the basic reductive explanation effect for psychological phenomena found in Hopkins et al. (2016). Our failure to replicate the original reductive explanation effect in Experiment 2 was complicated by the fact that we encountered abnormally high rates of participant exclusion based on our pre-registered criteria (namely, failure on the instructions, failure on our attention check, or submission times ±3 SD away from the mean). Out of the 174 participants who completed the survey, 82 were removed, resulting in an exclusion rate greater than 40%. This excessively high exclusion rate raises serious concern about the quality of our data, even for the participants who were not excluded. As such, our inability to replicate Hopkins et al. (2016) may have resulted from a generally inattentive participant pool. To address this concern, we will attempt a third replication of Hopkins et al. (2016). In this third replication, we will use the same procedure as described in Experiment 2 (osf.io/8af7k), however, we will recruit MTURK participants using CloudResearch, a third-party website that pre-screens MTURK workers to improved data quality. In this way, we will limit our recruitment to “approved” workers that are more likely to produce high-quality data with an acceptable exclusion rate.

title_r: Exact replication of Kozłowska et al. (2023) The Napoleon complex, revisited: Those high on the Dark Triad traits are dissatisfied with their height and are short
abstract_r: The dark triad is a personality taxonomy that, unlike the Big Five, focuses primarily on negative social personality traits: Psychopathy, Narcissism, and Machiavellianism. It has attracted much attention over the past 20 years after Paulhurst et al. coined the term in 2002, and research on the correlation between Dark Triad traits and other factors has increased drastically. One such example is the correlation of the Dark Triad traits with height dissatisfaction and with physical height itself. Kozłowska et al. recently published these results (2023) and concluded that the theory of the so-called "Napoleon complex" seems to be correct. Briefly summarized, the "Napoleon complex" is the idea that smaller men are at a disadvantage and compensate for this through negative behavior. In their results, Kozłowska et al. found that there was a significant negative correlation between Dark Triad traits and height in men. They also found that those scoring high on Dark Triad traits are more dissatisfied with their own height. This is interesting because it is one of the first studies to examine the relationship between Dark Triad traits and attitudes towards height, as well as physical height. Other studies of height in psychology often show no, or a positive, correlation. Therefore, it is of interest to conduct an exact replication study to verify or reject these findings in order to strengthen the current evidence base and thus lay the groundwork for further research on this topic.

title_r: Acquiring false information from narrative fictions: A conceptual replication and extension of Appel & Richter (2007)
abstract_r: Within the planned study, narrative fictions are understood as written stories that primarily deal with non-real events, objects and persons, whereby this limited reference to reality is both intended by the author and recognized by the recipients (e.g., Gertken & Köppe, 2009). Although people often encounter narrative fictions in everyday life, relatively little empirical research has been conducted on their psychological effects and the underlying mechanisms. Existing studies show that factually incorrect information embedded in narrative fictions can cause substantial changes in readers' beliefs despite the known limited reference to reality (e.g., Rapp et al., 2014). In one of the few studies on the topic that includes more than one measurement point, Appel and Richter (2007) demonstrated that such changes in belief can even increase over time – a phenomenon that corresponds to an absolute sleeper effect. Here, 81 participants recruited through a university (mostly students) read either a fictional story that contained both true and false claims about real-world issues, or a control story. There were great short-term persuasion effects from the false information; these effects were even greater in a group with a 2-week measurement delay. Belief certainty (i.e., how sure the readers were of their beliefs) was reduced immediately after reading, but returned to the baseline level after 2 weeks. The pattern of findings was interpreted in such a way that beliefs acquired through reading fictional narratives are integrated into world knowledge. The aim of the planned experiment is a conceptual replication and extension of this study. The experiment is planned to be identical to the original study except for two major differences: first, the participants will not be recruited at a university only in order that the generalizability of findings extends to a broader population; secondly, different reading stimuli (based on an excerpt from Homer's Odyssey) will be used than in Appel and Richter (2007). This will help clarify whether the findings occur independently of this specific textual material.

title_r: Are STEM Faculty Biased Against Female Applicants? A Robust Replication and Extension of Moss-Racusin and Colleagues (2012)
abstract_r: In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through three studies--one direct replication, one extension, and a meta-analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. The pre-registered data analysis plans will provide a strong test assessing the replicability of Moss-Racusin et al. (2012)’s finding that STEM faculty were biased against women who applied for a lab manager position.

title_r: Prevalence-induced Concept Change in the Judgement of Male Bodies: A Replication and Extension of Devine et al. (2023)
abstract_r: The following study aims to replicate H1b from Devine et al. (2023). Here, the authors found that men were sensitive to prevalence-induced concept changes (PICC) when judging whether male bodies varying in muscularity were muscular or not, but not when judging whether male bodies varying in body fat were overweight or not. Furthermore, they found that men were overall faster in judging whether a body is muscular compared to judging whether a body is overweight. Taken together, these results lead the authors to suspect that men might have an attentional bias towards idealized male bodies, which manifests in faster and more selective extraction of muscle-related body information. Thus, Devine et al. show that PICC may not represent a general perceptual effect, but rather could be moderated by the specific stimulus category. Our main goal of the current study is to replicate the effect found that the strength of PICC in the judgment of male bodies depends on the specific stimulus category (weight-related, muscle-related). Furthermore, we intend to replicate the difference in response times between the judgments of these stimulus categories. The study design will be adjusted to control for possible confounding factors such as the order of the presented stimulus category. In addition, the stimulus material (computer-generated male bodies) will be adapted in order to achieve better comparability between the stimulus categories. Furthermore, we will examine whether the degree of body dissatisfaction (BD) related to different body characteristics (weight-related, muscle-related) influences whether participants judge muscle-related bodies faster than weight-related bodies, or vice versa. Recent studies suggest that attentional biases toward body-related stimuli specifically affect men with higher BD rather than the general population, and that the impact might differ depending on whether men experience more muscle-related or weight-related BD (Joseph et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2018; Porras-Garcia et al., 2020; Talbot & Saleme, 2022; Kirby et al., 2023). Therefore, BD will be measured separately for both stimulus categories (weight-related, muscle-related) (Ralph-Nearman & Filik, 2018).

title_r: Working memory capacity and the risky-choice framing effect: A preregistered replication and extension of Corbin et al. (2010)
abstract_r: Higher working memory capacity is associated with superior performance on a number of tasks but may it sometimes be paradoxically associated with suboptimal performance? Corbin et al. (2010) found that, in a between-subjects design, higher WMC is associated with a larger risky-choice framing effect, traditionally conceived of as a departure from rational principles. Such surprising findings are of potentially great theoretical importance, yet the original study was underpowered. In this registered report, we aim to replicate and extend the original findings, by conducting an online experiment among 400 participants. To extend the findings beyond the specific single tasks used in the original study, we use three WMC tasks with different processing components and six framing problems involving human lives.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Fritz et al. (2010), from the Journal of Organizational Behavior - Direct Replication - k17
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Fritz et al. (2010) is that relaxation during the weekend is positively associated with joviality [at the end of the following week], which reflects the following statement from the abstract: "Hierarchical regression analyses revealed that after controlling for affective states the previous week, recovery experiences during the weekend significantly explained variance in affective states at the end of the weekend and during the following workweek." The claim is tested with data from a longitudinal survey of preschool teachers by regressing participants’ joviality at the end of the workweek on their level of relaxation during the previous weekend and their joviality before the previous weekend, as well as measures of detachment, mastery, control, and hassles (all during the previous weekend); and controls for age, gender, having children, work hours per week, and workdays per week. Relaxation significantly predicted joviality (β = 0.15, p < 0.01).

title_r: Conceptual replication of Ecker et al. (2015)
abstract_r: According to the so-called temporal gradient of retroactive interference (TGRI), retroactive interference effects are stronger the shorter the time interval between the original learning phase (L1) and an interpolated learning phase (L2). Because of the great theoretical importance of this effect, we intend to replicate two conditions of interest from Ecker et al. (2015, Experiment 1) in an online setting: the “short-long” condition (short L1-L2 interval, long L2-T interval) and the “long-short” condition (long L1-L2 interval, short L2-T interval). This will be done in a between-within interaction test that includes the data obtained by Ecker et al. (2015).

abstract_r: The goal of the current study was to conduct a conceptual replication of the reciprocal associations between executive function (EF) and academic achievement reported in Schmitt et al. (2017, https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000193). Using two independent samples (N (STAR) = 279, and N (Pathways) = 277), we examined whether the patterns of associations between EF and achievement across preschool and kindergarten reported in Schmitt et al. (2017) replicated using the same model specifications, similar EF and achievement measures, and across a similar developmental age period. Consistent with original findings, EF predicted subsequent math achievement in both samples. Specifically, in the STAR sample, EF predicted math achievement from preschool to kindergarten, and kindergarten to first grade. In the Pathways sample, EF at kindergarten predicted both math and literacy achievement in first grade. However, contrary to the original findings, we were unable to replicate the bidirectional associations between math achievement and EF in either of the replication samples. Overall, the current conceptual replication has revealed that bidirectional associations between EF and academic skills might not be robust to slight differences in EF measures and number of measurement occasions, which has implications for our understanding of the development EF and academic skills across early childhood. The present findings underscore the need for more standardization in both measurement and modeling approaches – without which the inconsistency of findings in published studies may continue across this area of research.

title_r: FT56.6 - Does Expressive Writing Blunt the Effects of Math Anxiety on Math Performance? A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Park et al. (2014)
abstract_r: Abstract: Math anxiety (MA) is negatively related to math performance. One proposed intervention with potential to disrupt the MA-math performance link is expressive writing. The current study aimed to conceptually replicate Park and colleagues (2014). In that study, the authors concluded that expressive writing effectively boosted math anxious students’ performance. In our current sample of 168 college students, participants randomly assigned to the expressive writing condition were no more accurate at posttest than were other participants assigned to a math self-concept intervention, active control, or passive control. Additionally, participants in the math self-concept and active control conditions reported lower state MA immediately following the intervention; participants in the expressive writing and passive control conditions reported no differences between pretest and posttest state MA. The current study provides boundary conditions for the effectiveness of expressive writing interventions in ameliorating MA during difficult math tasks and illuminates potential mechanisms underlying MA. title_r: Modeling Help Seeking Intentions In Victims Of Intimate Partner Violence: A Conceptual Replication Of Fleming And Resick (2017)
abstract_r: Victims of intimate partner violence come forward and seek services and help for the crimes committed upon them at much lower rates than victims of other interpersonal crimes. In this study, the Theory of Planned Behavior was used to assess individual behavioral predictors of formal help-seeking in victims of intimate partner violence in order to better understand factors that promote or inhibit help-seeking in this vulnerable population, including victims’ attitudes about help seeking, the subjective norms they feel about help seeking, their perceived ability to get help, and the relationship these factors have with prior experiences. Partial support was found for the full Theory of Planned Behavior model predicting intentions for all resource types, with attitudes and perceived behavioral control predicting intentions for most resources, while norms rarely contributed to the variance. Prior experience was related to attitudes about several of the resources.
